title: Accurate Reconstruction of the Standard 12-Lead ECG from a Single Lead Based on Inherent Principles of ECG
reviewer_1_strengths: The central design choice of incorporating Einthoven’s and Goldberger’s relationships as explicit deterministic operations rather than leaving them to be implicitly learned is a reasonable and well-motivated departure from the prevailing end-to-end learning paradigm. Constraining the solution space with known physical relationships reduces the learning burden and enforces internal consistency among the reconstructed limb leads, and the ablation comparing AURORA with its pure learning-based variant (AURORA_{1to11}) supports this design choice. The three-stage decomposition (1-to-1 generation, vector operations, 6-to-6 generation) provides a clear separation of concerns. Each stage has a well-defined role with explicit interfaces between them, which is a notable improvement over monolithic end-to-end approaches whose failure modes are often difficult to diagnose. The reported results show consistent gains over competitive baselines on two independent datasets with different target diseases. On PTB-XL, AURORA reduces RMSE by 13.0% and DTW by 26.3% compared to the strongest baseline (ANN128); on CUSPH, the corresponding improvements are 14.0% and 12.6%. The consistency across different metrics, datasets, and disease contexts suggests that the observed improvements are not artifacts of a particular evaluation setting.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper frames its goal as “accurate reconstruction of the standard 12-lead ECG from a single measured lead,” but the information-theoretic content of what is actually produced warrants closer examination. In AURORA, Lead II is generated from Lead I through M_{1-to-1}, and the remaining four limb leads (III, aVR, aVL, aVF) are computed as linear combinations of Lead I and the generated Lead II. Consequently, all six limb leads provided to M_{6-to-6} are ultimately functions of Lead I alone. The four vector-derived leads, being linear combinations of two signals, contribute no additional independent information by construction; they are formally redundant with {L_I, L_II^gen}. The six precordial leads are then generated from this set, meaning that all eleven reconstructed leads trace back to a single measured signal. The IGUANA training procedure includes a source reconstruction phase (Eq. 6) with its corresponding loss ℓ^s_rec (Eq. 10). The ablation in Table 2(b) shows that removing this loss degrades RMSE from 0.127 to 0.144, but the mechanism underlying this improvement is not established. The authors’ stated rationale - that it “encourages faithful transformation” - leaves several alternative explanations unexamined: the loss may simply act as a regularizer achievable through simpler means; it may alleviate under-training of G by doubling gradient signal per step; or, most concerning, it may incentivize an unintended failure mode in which L_I information is encoded into perceptually inconspicuous components of L_II^gen, a form of steganography documented in cycle-consistent translation models (Chu et al. , 2017). Under this last interpretation, the cycle loss would inflate apparent reconstruction fidelity without improving physiological validity. There is also a tension with the representation consistency loss ℓ^s_con (Eq. 9), which already enforces alignment between latent codes of real and generated signals. It is unclear what additional constraint source reconstruction provides beyond invertibility of G on these aligned representations. Distinguishing among these explanations would require targeted analyses - such as perturbation sensitivity tests on L_II^gen or matched-complexity regularization baselines-that the paper does not provide. Key training details including the loss weights λ_gen, λ_rec, λ_con, learning rate, batch size, and number of epochs are not reported in the paper, which limits reproducibility and makes it difficult to assess whether baselines were tuned under comparable protocols.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1) Well-motivated integration of domain knowledge: The central idea of combining learning-based reconstruction with deterministic ECG vector operations is both intuitive and well grounded in electrophysiological principles. This reduces the learning burden while enforcing physiologically consistent relationships between limb leads, which is a meaningful design choice. 2) Clear and structured problem decomposition: The separation into limb lead reconstruction and precordial lead reconstruction is well justified and aligns with known geometric and physiological differences between lead types. This structured pipeline improves interpretability compared to fully end-to-end approaches. 3) Consistent empirical improvements across metrics and datasets: The method shows clear gains over multiple baselines on RMSE, DTW, and PCC across two benchmark datasets. The improvements are consistent rather than isolated to a single metric, strengthening the empirical claims. 4) Clinical relevance through downstream evaluation: The inclusion of disease prediction experiments using reconstructed ECG signals is a strong aspect of the paper. Demonstrating that diagnostic performance remains close to that of original 12-lead ECG signals provides evidence that the reconstruction preserves clinically meaningful information. 5) Thoughtful ablation studies: The paper includes ablations that directly validate the two core claims (hybrid strategy and staged reconstruction) as well as the contribution of different loss components, which helps support the design choices. 6) Good clarity and organization: The paper is well structured, with clearly stated claims (C1, C2), a coherent methodological pipeline, and logical progression from motivation to validation.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1) Limited methodological novelty at the modeling level: While the hybrid formulation is well motivated, the underlying learning components (e.g., U-Net-based generator, representation learning, two-phase reconstruction) are largely based on existing architectures and training strategies. The main novelty lies more in the integration of known principles than in fundamentally new modeling techniques. 2) Incremental nature relative to prior reconstruction approaches: The task of reconstructing 12-lead ECG from reduced leads has been extensively studied, and many prior works already explore deep learning-based lead translation. The proposed method improves performance, but the conceptual leap beyond prior work is somewhat limited. 3) Fairness of baseline comparisons is not fully clear: Some baselines are re-implemented due to lack of public code. While this is understandable, the paper does not provide sufficient detail to ensure that these implementations are fully comparable to the original methods, which introduces some uncertainty in the reported gains. 4) Limited analysis of robustness and generalization: The experiments focus on standard benchmark datasets, but do not explore robustness to noise, device variability, or domain shifts, which are important considerations for real-world wearable ECG scenarios. 5) Design choices could be better justified: Certain decisions, such as the selection of specific limb leads (e.g., reconstructing Lead II first), are empirically motivated but not deeply analyzed. A more thorough justification or comparison with alternative configurations would strengthen the methodological argument. 6) Reproducibility details are partially incomplete: Although the authors provide a code link and indicate that code will be released, some implementation details (e.g., training hyperparameters, exact preprocessing steps, and architecture specifics) are not fully described in the manuscript, which may hinder exact replication.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper formulates the ECG reconstruction problem not as a purely end-to-end generation task, but as a structured problem that leverages vector relationships inherent in ECG signals. It introduces a hybrid strategy in which only one limb lead is reconstructed through learning, while the remaining limb leads are derived analytically using physiological equations. The proposed IGUANA framework combines a lead representation learner with an AdaIN-based 1D U-Net generator and incorporates both source reconstruction and representation consistency into the training process. Comprehensive experiments are conducted on both PTB-XL and CUSPH, including comparisons with competing methods, claim validation, and loss ablation studies. The reconstructed 12-lead ECG also achieves AUROC and AUPRC values close to those of the original ECG in downstream disease prediction tasks.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The proposed method remains close to an integration of existing lead reconstruction frameworks with ECG-based analytical relationships, and therefore does not strongly highlight methodological novelty. The experimental setting fixes the input lead to Lead I and the auxiliary lead to Lead II, but provides limited validation of generalization across different lead configurations. The rationale for adopting the current 6-to-6 conditioning scheme in precordial lead reconstruction is not sufficiently compared with alternative design choices. Since the proposed approach follows a staged reconstruction pipeline, further analysis is required to examine the potential accumulation of reconstruction errors across stages. In addition, some competing methods rely on the authors’ own implementations, leaving potential bias due to differences in reproduction settings.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Novelty (R2-W1,2/R3-W1): The novelty of AURORA is at the reconstruction-formulation level, not in replacing the backbone with a more-complex architecture. Rather than reconstructing all missing leads once by learning-based translation, AURORA reconstructs only one additional limb lead, computes the remaining limb leads through deterministic vector operations, and reconstructs precordial leads conditioned on the full limb-lead set. This approach reduces the learning burden and constrains the output space to physiologically consistent ECGs, which is not achieved by simply applying a generic lead-translation network. We believe it is a meaningful methodological contribution to medical AI, aligned with recent MICCAI studies deriving values from domain knowledge or physiological/physical priors in reconstruction formulation [MRF-DiPh(MICCAI’25)/TA-fMRI-GM(MICCAI’25)/ACIS(MICCAI’24)]. We will clarify this positioning in the final version. 1-to-1 validation (R3-W2): Our target scenario is Lead-I-based reconstruction because many wearable/portable devices acquire a Lead-I-like signal [mECGNet(MICCAI’25)]. We agree that arbitrary input-lead generalization is broader, but it is not the focus of this submission. Within this setting, the auxiliary lead was not arbitrary: comparing candidate auxiliary limb leads, Lead II was most reliable, achieving 0.127/0.722 versus 0.203/0.519 in RMSE/PCC for the best alternative, Lead III. This supports the Lead-II choice as empirically justified and physiologically plausible, as Lead II often aligns with the dominant cardiac electrical axis. Lead I information (R1-W1): We agree with R1 that AURORA does not create independent information beyond measured Lead I. Rather, we view it as diagnostic-view augmentation: Lead I may contain disease-relevant cues, but these can be difficult for downstream models to exploit from a single directional view. Since ECG leads reflect the same cardiac activity from different directions, AURORA presents such cues in the standard 12-lead form. To test whether the gain comes from Lead I itself, we added a Lead I-only baseline in this rebuttal; it achieved AUROC 0.87/0.78, lower than AURORA and prior reconstruction baselines. Error accumulation (R3-W3): We agree that a staged pipeline could introduce error accumulation, particularly for precordial leads. To examine this directly, we evaluated V1–V6 only, beyond the 11-lead average in Table 2.On V1–V6, AURORA achieved 0.16/0.76 in RMSE/PCC, outperforming AURORA_{1to11} (0.18/0.62). This suggests that structured limb-lead conditioning benefits precordial reconstruction and is not dominated by possible error propagation. Cycle concerns (R1-W2,3): We agree that source reconstruction may raise steganography or gradient-doubling concerns. However, unlike unpaired cycle-consistent translation, the generated Lead II is directly supervised by paired ground-truth Lead II. As a sanity check, 40Hz low-pass filtering generated Lead II before source reconstruction changed RMSE/PCC only marginally from 0.316/0.941 to 0.317/0.940, suggesting no strong reliance on fragile high-frequency hidden signals. A matched gradient-doubling baseline without source reconstruction achieved 0.328/0.884, still worse than AURORA. Thus, the gain is not simply explained by hidden channels or doubled gradients. Reproducibility/baselines (R1-W4/R2-W3,6/R3-W4): We appreciate the concerns regarding AURORA reproducibility and baseline fairness. We updated the missing AURORA training/preprocessing details, including hyperparameters, in the anonymous repository. Since official implementations of several baselines were unavailable, we followed the original papers and updated the anonymous repository with reproduced baseline implementations and training configurations. Naming (R1): IGUANA is an acronym of multI-lead ECGs Generation throUgh leAd patterN leArning. We apologize for the confusion and will revise it accordingly.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This is a interesting study which employs the intrinsic physiological principles of ECG signals to reconstruct 12-lead ECG. The method is simple but intuitive and reasonable. Some minor issue raised by the reviewers need to be solved further | I am happy with the rebuttal, which solved my concerns. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Major concerns from the reviewers have been addressed. It is not clear whether the newly added baseline and “low-pass filtering and gradient-double checks” involved any possible violation of MICCAI’s rebuttal rules, and these updates were not in the manuscript. Based on the updated reviews and meta-reviews, I recommend a plain-poster presentation binding the following camera-ready conditions: “Analyses provided in the rebuttal should be clearly reflected in the final manuscript” – R3, these include: 1.Lead-I-only baseline, the V1 to V6 error-accumulation breakdown, and the low-pass and matched gradient-doubling sanity checks 2.Report the training hyperparameters, preprocessing, and baseline-reproduction settings now held only in the repository. 3.define the IGUANA acronym at first use (critical) Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Rebuttal answered questions, remaining issues with R3 are non-fatal. “Cautiously optimistic” with respect to novelty, but certainly worth acceptance.

title: CoSim: Unleashing Eye Movements for EEG-Free Emotion Recognition via Conditional Prompting and Similarity-Guided Augmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The concept of the conditional prompting generator is interesting and one of the potential strengths of the contribution if validated properly. Likewise the proposed similarity guided augmentation is an interesting concept that could translate to other use cases beyond the one considered.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: My main issue is the limited sample size in the SEED datasets that were used to validate the approaches. Authors have described how they select similar subjects and also how the CPG is trained to generate EEG data but it is unclear how this would translate to a real world setting with more than 15 or 20 subjects. In other words, it could be that the subjects in the SEED study are very similar and that the model simply learns to predict the same average patterns. The accuracy achieved is certainly good but to truly judge the significance of these results it would be helpful to analyze the differences in feature distributions in the train and test sets. How different are they really? Can the models really generalize to subjects which have a different EYE - EEG response?
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1) The paper addresses a relevant and practically motivated problem: reducing dependence on EEG at test time while still exploiting EEG during training. This is an important direction because EEG acquisition is cumbersome, whereas eye tracking is substantially more accessible. The motivation is clearly stated, and the test-time setting is meaningful. (2) The paper presents a reasonably coherent system design rather than a single isolated trick. The combination of multimodal pretraining, conditional pseudo-feature generation, subject-aware data augmentation, and a specialized transformer backbone is well organized and easy to follow in Fig. 1 and the method section. In particular, the distinction between pretraining, personalized finetuning, and EYE-only inference is clearly described. (3) Under the chosen protocol, the method outperforms several prior cross-modal baselines and also compares favorably to some EEG-only and full-modality baselines. The ablation study also suggests that CPG, SKA, and FET each contribute positively to performance. (4) The feature visualization and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis for SKA support the intuition behind the framework and make the paper more complete experimentally.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: （1) The authors claim the approach aims to “enhance the inference-time performance” of the EYE modality in the abstract. However, the experimental section primarily reports static accuracy on standard datasets. To truly demonstrate “enhanced inference-time performance” in a way that justifies the complexity of CPG, the authors should provide a more detailed analysis of the computational overhead and latency incurred by pseudo-feature generation during inference relative to standard EYE-only models. (2) The proposed CPG module functions primarily as a statistical feature translator. However, it fails to leverage explicit neurophysiological priors governing the EEG-EYE relationship (e.g., the coupling between saccadic eye movements and specific neural oscillations). The authors should clarify how the FET backbone or CPG specifically aligns with known physiological mechanisms rather than relying solely on adversarial alignment. (3) The novelty of SKA is not fully convincing, and its effectiveness remains insufficiently validated. The idea of selecting top-K similar subjects based on prototype similarity and then performing weighted sampling is intuitive. Still, it appears closer to a standard neighbor-based augmentation strategy than to a genuinely new formulation. More importantly, the paper does not compare SKA with simpler alternatives, such as class-balanced augmentation or EYE-only nearest-neighbor matching. Since SKA is intended to reduce overfitting, stronger evidence is needed to show that the similarity criterion itself matters.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1) The authors developed Conditional Prompting Generator (CPG) that generates pseudo-EEG representations conditioned on the EYE input. 2) They also Similarity-Guided Knowledge Augmentation (SKA) aimed to reduce CPG overfitting. 3) They developed and ML model using Fourier-Enhanced Transformer (FET) Backbone, achieving higher accuracy than the state-of-the-art in the literature.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Although the paper is excellently written and is publishable in its current form. There are few correction that would further improve it. 1) In section 2.1 the authors forgot to define the lambda components of their equations. 2) The authors should soften the claim in Section 2.3: “To mitigate this, we propose SKA strategy that regularizes training by leveraging data from similar subjects.” to “To mitigate this, we propose SKA strategy that aims to regularize training by leveraging data from similar subjects.”, because the earlier sentence presents the effect as established, whereas this is not necessarily guaranteed. Although augmenting a target subject’s training set with data from similar subjects may improve generalization, it may also introduce bias or encourage the model to fit subject-specific patterns, depending on how similarity is defined and how the augmentation is performed. 3) In the third sentence of Section 2.4, the authors should revise “Inspired by FAN [1], …” to “Inspired by Fourier Analysis Networks (FAN) [1], …” since this is the first occurrence of the acronym. 4) The first sentence in the third paragraph of Section 2.4 should be revised from “By applying this structure to the Query, Key, and Value projections, …” to “By applying this structure to the Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) projections, …”. This would make the connection to Equation (10) clearer for the reader. 5) In the Dataset subsection of Section 3.1, the authors should cite the original sources of the SEED and SEED-IV datasets. This is important both to properly acknowledge the dataset creators and to help readers easily locate the data. 6) The claim (in the second sentence of Section 3.3) that removing SKA makes the model “prone to overfitting” is not sufficiently supported by the reported mean accuracy +/- standard deviation alone. A performance drop only indicates that SKA contributes positively under the evaluated setting, but it does not by itself establish overfitting as the cause. To support such a claim, the authors should provide additional evidence, such as training vs. validation/test performance, loss curves, or explicit generalization-gap analysis. Otherwise, the statement should be softened to indicate reduced robustness or degraded generalization rather than overfitting (as the authors did with CPG in the first sentence).
reviewer_3_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
author_feedback: We thank the Meta Reviewer (Meta) and reviewers for constructive feedback and acknowledging our novelty. Due to the double-blind policy, the code will be open-sourced upon acceptance. Responses to core concerns follow: [Meta, R1] Generalization & Train/Test Shift: SEED is a standard benchmark; its original paper [Zheng & Lu, IEEE TAMD ‘15] confirms significant cross-subject variability. The t-SNE plots in Fig. 3a/b show CPG-generated features avoid mode collapse and don’t degrade to a static mean, capturing dynamic physiological changes. The train/test sets also use distinct video stimuli. Due to signal non-stationarity and stimulus disparity, a significant distribution shift inherently exists. Maintaining high accuracy here proves our model extracts domain-invariant features and universal physiological laws, demonstrating robust generalization. Broad-scenario generalization will be verified via large-scale multi-center datasets in future work. [Meta, R2] Inference Cost: During inference, CPG only executes a lightweight generator, adding marginal constant-time (O(1)) overhead compared to GANs. Profiling logs on SEED show pseudo-feature generation adds just 2.14 ms latency (total inference per sample is 3.22 ms). We trade 2.14 ms latency and increased parameters (from 97.4k to 1.5M) for an accuracy leap from 84.90% to 98.52% (Tab. 2b). This boosts performance at an acceptable delay, fully satisfying real-time deployment needs. A detailed time analysis will be added. [Meta, R2] Physiological Interpretation: Neuroscience confirms EYE-EEG coupling via: (1) periodic rhythmic synchronization (e.g., saccade-EEG phase-locking [Staudigl et al., PLoS Biol. ‘17]); (2) aperiodic state covariation (e.g., pupil-arousal mapping to 1/f EEG background [Joshi et al., Neuron ‘16; Donoghue et al., Nat. Neurosci. ‘20]). Leveraging this prior, CPG (Eqs. 1, 2) converts eye-movement cues into conditional prompts, providing initial cross-modal guidance. Since neural rhythms and aperiodic baselines are highly temporally entangled, FET (Eqs. 7, 8) mathematically enforces signal decoupling via the frequency domain. Features are strictly partitioned into periodic subspaces (saccades mapped to neural oscillations) and aperiodic subspaces (pupil-linked arousal baselines). This structural constraint avoids blind data-driven mapping, explicitly ensuring biological plausibility. Thus, our architectural design is driven by these neurophysiological priors. [Meta, R2] SKA Mechanism & Baselines: We carefully considered this during design. Our goal is to extract data with deep physiological similarity, not mere volume augmentation. Conventional class-balanced augmentation introduces heterogeneous noise, while eye-only nearest-neighbor search suffers from signal sparsity. Thus, SKA uses information-rich joint EEG-EYE features to build a similarity matrix during training, overcoming these issues and outperforming both baselines. Fig. 3c further validates this: as neighbor count k increases, including low-similarity subjects causes a noticeable accuracy drop. This confirms that blind augmentation introduces interference, making SKA’s precise matching optimal. [Meta, R2, R3] “Overfitting” Clarification: We agree a simple accuracy drop doesn’t rigorously prove overfitting. However, an analysis of the training curves (from the training and test loss logs) reveals SKA reduces the generalization gap by 60.7% on average. This mechanistically confirms that SKA substantially improves generalization ability, indicating the baseline drop involves overfitting factors. To ensure academic rigor, we will use more precise terminology. For example, following R3’s suggestion, we will replace ‘overfitting’ with ‘degraded generalization’ and ‘reduced robustness’. [R3] We will adopt all suggestions: (1) clearly define λ in Sec. 2.1; (2) tone down the assertion in Sec. 2.3 to “aims to regularize”; (3) provide full names for FAN and Q/K/V at first use; (4) add original dataset citations.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper addresses a practical problem of EEG-free emotion recognition by using paired EEG-EYE data during training and only EYE signals at inference. The proposed CoSim framework combines a Conditional Prompting Generator, Similarity-Guided Knowledge Augmentation, and a Fourier-Enhanced Transformer, and reviewers generally acknowledge the clear motivation, coherent design, and promising empirical results. I recommend inviting a rebuttal. The authors should mainly address the following points: clarify whether the method can generalize beyond the small SEED/SEED-IV subject pools and provide analysis of train/test feature distribution differences; report the inference-time overhead and latency introduced by pseudo-EEG generation; better justify the physiological basis of the EEG-EYE relationship modeled by CPG and FET; strengthen the validation of SKA by comparing with simpler alternatives such as class-balanced augmentation or EYE-only nearest-neighbor matching; and soften unsupported claims about overfitting unless training/validation curves or generalization-gap analyses are provided. Overall, the paper has clear merit, but the rebuttal should focus on dataset generalization, practical inference cost, physiological interpretation, and stronger evidence for the proposed SKA mechanism. | This paper addresses a practical and meaningful problem by enabling EYE-only emotion recognition at inference time while using paired EEG-EYE data during training. The proposed CoSim framework is clearly organized, combining conditional pseudo-EEG generation, similarity-guided subject augmentation, and a Fourier-enhanced backbone, and the reported results, ablation study, visualization, and sensitivity analysis provide reasonable support for its effectiveness. After rebuttal, two reviewers support acceptance, including one reviewer who changed from weak reject to accept, while one reviewer maintains concerns about the strength of the physiological interpretation, the novelty of SKA, and the increased parameter size. I consider these concerns valid but not fatal; they mainly require clearer positioning and limitation discussion rather than rejection. Therefore, I recommend acceptance, with the expectation that the authors revise the camera-ready version to soften claims about explicit neurophysiological grounding, clearly report inference latency and parameter size, clarify the role and novelty of SKA, cite the original SEED and SEED-IV datasets, and avoid unsupported statements about overfitting. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): I tend to agree more with R2.The paper has some merit in terms of the proposed framework and strong performance. The rebuttal, however, does not adequately address some of the major concerns regarding insufficient novelty and validation. With substantially high computational overhead at test time and lacking generalization beyond the specific data distribution (SEED), it is difficult to justify an acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): There were several points raised by the reviewers: The generalisation of the method to other datasets, practical deployment of the model, a justification for the method tied to the physiology, The others attempted to answer these concerns. The authors response related to the prior underpinning does seem overstated based on what the experimental design can show versus the thinking. However the experiments and approach overall seem interesting and novel even if some of the interpretation of what the method is doing is likely overstated. I would suggest the authors think carefully about what they can actually demonstrate and keep those points in while removing or softening language for elements they believe are encoding specific types of information but have no evidence for. The inference speed, and small sample size were both address well in the rebuttal.

title: Cross-Modal Concept Transfer: From ECG Signals to Images for Explainable Disease Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The method is innovative and practical. It transforms the existing concept bottleneck model into a cross-modal version specially for ECG analysis. 2.The idea is easy to follow. The model provides clear quantitative results that match medical standards and can be easily understood by doctors. It supports both ECG images and signal inputs, making it very flexible and suitable for real clinical use.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The model relies on a relatively limited set of features. It only uses basic ECG intervals and heart rate variability features, without including more important high-level indicators such as ST-T morphology that are widely used in clinical diagnosis. This limits the model’s ability to represent complex cardiac conditions. 2.All experiments use synthetic ECG images, and the model has not been tested on real scanned ECGs from clinical settings. As a result, its generalization ability in real-world scenarios remains unclear and needs further verification.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical problem: the discrepancy between signal-based ECG modeling and real-world settings where only ECG images are available. The proposed idea is interesting and well-motivated. Extending Concept Bottleneck Models to a cross-modal setting using signal-derived physiological concepts is a natural and meaningful contribution. The method provides quantitative interpretability, going beyond standard qualitative explanations. The use of clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., waveform intervals, HRV metrics) is particularly compelling. The framework is well-designed and clearly described. The integration of concept supervision into image representation learning is intuitive and supported by the architecture (Fig. 1). Experimental results are solid: the method consistently improves over image-based baselines and achieves performance comparable to signal-based models (Table 1) . Additional analyses, such as concept intervention and robustness across backbones, strengthen the empirical evaluation.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Limited ablation studies: While the results are strong, the paper lacks a detailed ablation analysis to disentangle the contribution of each component. In particular, it would be important to evaluate: (i) an image-only variant without concept supervision, and (ii) a signal-only or concept-only variant, to better quantify the benefit of cross-modal concept transfer. Code availability is unclear or incomplete: Although a GitHub link is provided, it appears to be empty at the time of review. This raises concerns about reproducibility and should be addressed. Some design choices are insufficiently justified: For example, the use of SmoothL1 (Huber) loss for concept regression and the EMA-based dynamic loss weighting are reasonable, but not well motivated or compared against alternatives. Limited discussion of limitations: The method assumes access to paired signal-image data during training, which may not always be available. This constraint is not sufficiently discussed.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The proposed framework is intuitive, enables interpretability, and allows for flexible selection of inference-time input modality (either signal or image). The authors also demonstrate that their approach facilitates clinically valid explanations without significantly sacrificing performance. The paper is well-written and the contribution is valuable.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Please find below a list of issues the authors should address. Most of these issues are minor, but addressing would help strengthen the work. 1.In the abstract, the authors motivate the importance of using a cross-modal framework by stating that electrocardiograms (ECGs) are often stored as images without preserving the raw signals. However, it does not appear as though the authors tested the robustness of their CMCT approach on such real-world ECG images, which may have quality and consistency issues. Instead, the authors use ECG-Image-Kit to render waveforms into a consistent image format. Is there a reason the authors didn’t consider such an analysis? 2.When describing the Exponential Moving Average-based dynamic loss-weighting strategy, the authors discuss three parameters, alpha, epsilon, and p, used in equations (3)-(5). The tradeoffs of each parameters (i.e., the effect of a low vs high value) are discussed, but the authors do not state which values they used or if they performed hyperparameter tuning to select the optimal values. 3.How did the authors chose the four state-of-the-art signal-based baselines (ST-MEM, MERL, HeartLang, and MELP)? Did the authors consider ECG foundation models such as HuBERT-ECG [r1], ECGFounder [r2], ECG-FM [r3], and ECG-KED [r4]? Why or why not? 4.Just to clarify, the authors don’t train any signal-based model to predict concepts, is this correct? From my understanding, if someone wants to use the raw signal during inference, they would calculate/extract the concepts using NeuroKit2 then pass these concepts through the concept classifier? To me, it seems the approach is more of a simple extension of the Concept Bottleneck Model (with continuous instead of binary concepts and automatically calculated instead of human-annotated concepts) and less of a cross-modal approach, since the modeling only happens with the image modality. The contribution is still valuable, because the concepts are derived from direct signals only, but it would be helpful for the authors to articulate what they mean by cross-modal. 5.Table 1: I think parts (a) and (b) of the table should be combined to avoid repeating the final row. For part (b), why didn’t the authors compare their direct signal-to-concept modality for comparison with the signal-based baselines? It appears the authors only show results for the image-to-concept modality. 6.In 3.4 (Intervening on AF), the authors only show 2 examples of test-time intervention fixing the final classification (Fig. 3). author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive suggestions and positive evaluation of our work. We provide our responses to the reviewers’ comments below. 1.[MR, R3.4] Clarification of cross-modal design: Cross-Modal Concept Transfer (CMCT) is indeed related to the Concept Bottleneck Model (CBM) paradigm, as described in Section 2, but we would like to clarify that it is not merely a CBM with continuous concepts. In conventional image-based CBMs, concepts usually represent visual or semantic attributes that can be directly observed from the input image, such as object parts, colors, or textures. Therefore, the concept space mainly structures or disentangles the visual information already present in the image. In contrast, CMCT does not use concepts to simply describe visual attributes of ECG images, such as the presence or absence of a waveform pattern. Instead, it uses continuous physiological measurements extracted from the raw ECG signal, such as intervals and rhythm-related measurements. These concepts provide signal-level quantitative supervision that is not explicitly available as image-level visual labels. This is the key sense in which CMCT is cross-modal. The image encoder is trained with ECG images as input, but its representation is guided toward physiological information derived from the signal modality. Thus, the concept space acts not only as an interpretable bottleneck, but also as a signal-to-image transfer bridge: it transfers signal-derived physiological information into the image representation, rather than merely reinforcing visual attributes. As a result, the learned image representation becomes signal-informed, which supports both improved localization in ECG images and clinically meaningful concept-level explanations. We will clarify this in the camera-ready version. 2.[MR, R2.2, R2.3, R3.2] Clarification of experimental design: First, we used the SmoothL1, or Huber, loss for concept transfer because the physiological ECG concepts have different numerical scales and sensitivities. The Huber loss is commonly used as a robust regression loss, which helps stabilize optimization when jointly learning multiple continuous concepts with heterogeneous value ranges. Second, for the EMA-based dynamic loss weighting, we also considered simpler alternatives, including an unweighted sum and fixed weighted combinations, but these require manually setting the relative importance of concept learning and disease prediction. Since the two losses can have different scales and learning dynamics, a fixed design may cause one objective to dominate the other. Therefore, we adopted the EMA-based strategy to adaptively balance the two objectives and stabilize joint learning. Regarding the hyperparameters, we will make them available by reporting them in the final version of the paper and in the GitHub repository released with the camera-ready version. 3.[R1.1, R1.2, R3.1] Clinical generalization: The physiological concepts used in our study were selected as representative ECG features based on clinical expertise. We agree that higher-level indicators, such as ST-T morphology, could further enrich the concept space, and we consider this an important direction for future work. For ECG images, we used ECG-Image-Kit under a setting designed to resemble real clinical ECG records. We acknowledge that hospital-scanned ECGs may sometimes contain stronger artifacts and quality variations, making external validation on real scanned ECG images an important future direction. 4.[R2.4] Data requirements: CMCT is trained using signal-derived concepts, and if such concepts are stored in clinical data systems, they can be used for training even when raw signals are unavailable. Once trained, CMCT allows flexible inference with the available modality, without requiring paired signal-image data. 5.[R3.7] Typo: We thank the reviewer for carefully pointing this out and will correct it in the camera-ready version.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We address the major concerns below. (New experiments not included as per MICCAI guidelines) [R1, R2, R4] Single-Participant Scope: We acknowledge this limitation; however, microelectrode recordings of the speech motor cortex are rare and small-scale. The alternative datasets suggested use ECoG/fMRI/EEG, which operate on fundamentally different spatial and temporal scales than microelectrode arrays, making direct comparison out of scope. Both methods are biologically motivated to generalize across patients: NCS: Electrodes are implanted specifically in speech motor cortex, so recorded signals primarily reflect articulatory movements rather than higher-level semantic content — making word-level signatures structurally stable and reusable across rearrangements for any patient. ADAN: Drift from micro-motions and glial scarring is a universal constraint of intracortical BCIs. ADAN models this as a statistical domain shift, adversarially enforcing session-invariant representations regardless of individual neural patterns. [R2, R4] NCS Signal Dynamics & Continuity: Cuts occur strictly within long BLANK/SPACE regions where co-articulatory coupling is minimal. Signal reconstruction applies mean/variance alignment and spectral crossfading at boundaries to suppress discontinuities. Additionally, 2,000 randomized word sequences regularize against the model exploiting linguistic structure in place of neural dynamics. The 10.1%→8.8% PER reduction empirically confirms the net benefit. [R4] Prior Augmentation Literature: Existing microelectrode array augmentation methods primarily use time shifting/warping, noise injection and channel/time masking; to our knowledge, none improved PER/WER over baseline metrics. We acknowledge the absence of a formal comparative study as a limitation. [R1, R4] Generative Branch: Motivation & Interpretation: The generator was trained on the original 40-hour dataset using Soft-DTW and CTC-consistency losses (Table 1 will be updated). It was designed to model co-articulatory context by inverting sentence-level phoneme sequences back into continuous neural signals — an explicit attempt to go beyond NCS’s static word-segment assumption. We retained it to transparently document this exploration. Its inferior performance stems from compounding failure modes: the inversion starts from soft-logits carrying 10.1% inherent decoder error; the CTC training signal depends on this same imperfect decoder; and Soft-DTW optimizes a soft minimum over alignments rather than a single ground-truth path, introducing path-averaging artifacts. Together, these produce spectral artifacts that explains the large performance gap. [R4] GRL Clarification: The GRL is not a skip connection — it sits sequentially between the statistical pooling layer and the day classifier. During backpropagation, gradients pass through the pooling layer to the encoder with their sign negated by the GRL, suppressing day-specific information while preserving phonetic structure. We will clarify this in Figure 3. [R1, R4] Architecture & OPT-6.7B During development we evaluated biGRU, biLSTM, and standard RNN architectures; the GRU consistently outperformed alternatives. It also enables a direct 1-to-1 comparison with the official benchmark baseline, ensuring reported WER gains reflect solely our neural decoding contributions. Both NCS and ADAN are architecture-agnostic; multi-backbone evaluation is flagged as future work. [R1] Training Protocol Models were trained for a fixed number of epochs on merged train+validation data; the optimal epoch count was determined on per-session validation splits in a preliminary run. The held-out test session was never used for tuning. We will make this explicit in the final manuscript. [R4] Figure Clarity: Legend overlap in Figure 4 will be corrected. Code will be made public upon acceptance.

author_feedback: General Response to All Reviewers: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We agree that further evaluations are vital. However, due to MICCAI’s strict 8-page limit, we carefully scoped this submission as a foundational proof-of-concept. What separates our approach from prior ECG SSM models is our unique dual attention aggregation mechanism, which ensures robustness against varying signal durations and missing leads, coupled with a flexible integration mechanism for tabular metadata. Specific concerns are addressed below. ——- 1.Baselines, Dataset Selection, and Future Cohorts (Reviewers 1 & 2) Critique: Missing comparisons to Transformers and SSM-based models, and limited external generalization. Response: We acknowledge the omission of recent parallel SSM works and will add references to ECGMamba, S2M2ECG, and MSECG in the revision. We selected the 1D-ResNet as our primary baseline because it is the seminal architecture published alongside the CODE and SaMi-Trop datasets, enabling a direct and rigorous comparison on the exact same data splits. Furthermore, validating the prognostic value of ECG-age requires large-scale datasets linked with long-term mortality data, which exclude public sets like PTB-XL. Because SaMi-Trop is a severe-pathology cohort (Chagas cardiomyopathy) with double the mortality rate of the training data, a domain gap and performance drop are expected. To address this and conduct broader validations, we are applying for data access to the Harvard-Emory ECG Database (10M ECGs), the SHIP and HNR cohorts (Germany), and MIMIC-IV. Extensive benchmarking against recent Transformers and SSMs on these diverse cohorts is underway for a journal extension. 2.Clinical Utility vs. MAE (Reviewers 2 & 3) Critique: Is a drop in MAE clinically meaningful given the 8-year threshold? Could this cause misclassification? Response: We understand the concern regarding prediction noise near the 8-year threshold. However, the MAE reduction (8.44 to 6.72) is coupled with a substantial variance reduction (SD dropped from 7.12 to 5.81). This tighter error distribution means fewer patients are misclassified across the ±8-year boundary due to random noise. This precision drives our statistical improvement in risk stratification (HRs for all-cause mortality improved from 1.80 to 2.06). We will clarify that ECG-age is intended as an adjunctive screening flag in routine exams, not a standalone diagnostic, mitigating false alarm risks 3.The “Multimodal” Label (Reviewers 2 & 3) Critique: “Multimodal” is overstated since the only non-ECG input is biological sex. Response: We agree that utilizing only biological sex limits the traditional scope of “multimodal.” Our intention was to propose a foundational architecture capable of deep metadata fusion that can scale with high-dimensional metadata (e.g., extensive comorbidities) in future work. We will tone down the “multimodal” claims in the text and are open to adjusting the title (e.g., “Demographic-Conditioned”). 4.Technical Specifics: 400 Hz and Explainability (Reviewer 2) Critique: Why a 400 Hz sampling rate, and where are the attention visualizations? Response: 400 Hz Sampling Rate: While 500 Hz is standard clinically, 400 Hz is the native preprocessing standard established by the CODE dataset authors. To maintain strict comparability with the 1D-ResNet baseline, we adhered to the same dataset-specific sampling rate. Explainability: We agree visual explainability is crucial. However, merely overlaying attention weights onto ECG signals without rigorous clinical context can be misleading. Proper analysis requires carefully linking scores to established physiological ECG features. Due to the 8-page limit, we lacked the necessary space for this evaluation. A comprehensive interpretability analysis is a core component of our planned extended journal submission
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviews are mixed, with two weak-accept recommendations and one weak-reject recommendation. The paper presents a SSM/Mamba-based architecture for ECG-based age estimation, trained on a large CODE cohort and evaluated with both internal and external validation. The reviewers recognize several strengths, including the scale of the study, clear architecture, improved regression performance over a 1D-ResNet baseline, sex-conditioned versus sex-agnostic analysis, and the inclusion of survival analysis for prognostic relevance. However, the reviewers raise several important concerns. The main issues are: (1) the methodological novelty is incremental, and related recent ECG Mamba/SSM and Transformer-style baselines are not sufficiently discussed or compared; (2) the external validation results are weaker than the internal results, with limited R2 and less consistent prognostic significance on SaMi-Trop; (3) the clinical utility of the ECG-age gap remains insufficiently justified, especially given that the MAE is close to the 8-year prognostic threshold; and (4) the term “multimodal” may be overstated because the only non-ECG input is biological sex, and the interpretability claims based on attention are not yet supported by qualitative analysis. | After considering the reviews and rebuttal, I recommend acceptance. The rebuttal reasonably clarifies the baseline choice, the use of the CODE-standard 400 Hz sampling rate, the expected domain gap on SaMi-Trop, and the intended role of ECG-age as an adjunctive prognostic or screening signal rather than a standalone clinical decision tool. The authors also agree to tone down the “multimodal” framing. Important limitations remain, including incremental novelty, lack of recent Transformer/SSM ECG baselines, weaker external validation, and limited evidence for clinical actionability. Nevertheless, given the scale, reproducibility, external evaluation, and generally positive reviewer opinions, the paper is above the acceptance threshold. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Although evaluation with newer methods is mentioned, the reviewers concur that this is a paper with a comprehensive evaluation. The survival analysis is relevant for a clinical application of age estimation. My assessment is that the positive aspects outweigh the weaknesses, so I suggest acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This is an interesting and clinically relevant study, particularly in using ECG-age for mortality risk stratification and testing generalization in a severe-pathology cohort. Although the “multimodal” claim should be toned down and broader SSM/Transformer baselines would strengthen the work, the rebuttal reasonably addresses the main concerns, and the reported improvements in MAE, variance reduction, and hazard ratio suggest meaningful potential clinical value.

reviewer_2_strengths: This paper addresses the problem itself is genuinely meaningful. MCG is clinically promising, but systems based on SQUID or OPM are still expensive and cumbersome to deploy. From that perspective, improving the signal quality of low-cost TMR-based MCG is not just a technical exercise, but something that could actually matter in practice. This is problematic because it’s unclear whether DFuse is truly denoising the signal or simply learning to approximate a smoothed template. Without an independent clean reference, the performance gains on real data are difficult to validate. I also had some reservations about the simulated benchmark. The paper rightly points out that ECG and TMR-based MCG have different signal and noise characteristics, but the simulated data are still derived from PTB-XL ECG signals injected into a coil-based setup. This may be a practical approximation, but I am not fully convinced that it captures the complexity of real multi-channel MCG. Another point is that MGU-Net is discussed in the introduction as a relevant prior method for TMR-based MCG denoising, yet it is not included in the comparisons. I understand that it is a single-channel method, so the comparison would not be perfectly matched, but some form of discussion or adapted baseline would still have been useful. reviewer_3_strengths: The so-called innovation of this work largely remains at the level of engineering-style integration of existing dual-branch encoding, attention-based fusion, and channel reweighting modules, with only task-specific adaptation for TMR-MCG denoising.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) The overall writing is not sufficiently concise, which makes the presentation of the method motivation, the relationships among modules, and the core innovations insufficiently clear, thereby affecting readability. In addition, the manuscript still has some issues in terms of English writing quality and consistency, such as inconsistent capitalization, hyphenation, and terminology usage. 2) From a methodological perspective, the architectural contribution of this work appears rather limited. It is closer to a combinational integration of common components, such as dual-branch encoding, attention-based fusion, and channel reweighting, rather than a genuinely novel core mechanism. Although the authors apply the framework to the TMR-MCG denoising scenario, such task-specific adaptation alone is not sufficient to support a strong methodological contribution. This is especially the case given that TMR-based magnetocardiography has already seen continued research progress in recent years, while denoising itself is no longer a particularly frontier research topic. 3) The experimental comparison is still insufficient. The current baselines mainly include several deep learning models and conventional FIR/IIR and DWT methods, but coverage of analytical denoising approaches commonly used in clinical or engineering practice in the MCG/MEG field is clearly inadequate. At a minimum, the authors should discuss or compare against projection- and subspace-based methods (e.g., SSP, SSS, HFC, and tSSS), as well as filtering strategies based on reference sensors or environmental noise modeling. Compared with these methods, which are more commonly used in practice and have clearer physical interpretability, deep learning approaches are often less explainable. Therefore, comparison against only a limited set of baselines is not sufficient to fully demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method. 4) The paper also shows clear weaknesses in reproducibility. The manuscript does not clearly specify the loss function used for training, although this is a critical piece of information for any deep learning-based denoising method, and no explicit formula or description can be found in the method section. At the same time, important implementation details, such as training hyperparameters, optimizer settings, learning rate schedule, batch size, number of training epochs, and model selection criteria, are not sufficiently described, making it difficult for readers to reproduce the reported results. In addition, no code or pretrained model appears to be publicly available, which further weakens the verifiability of the work. 5) In Fig. 1, where is Fltw actually output? I could not identify its location in the diagram, although I later found from the text how it is derived. This point should be clarified more explicitly in the figure or in the accompanying explanation. 6) The core application goal of magnetocardiography is disease screening and pathological feature identification. However, the experiments in this paper are restricted to healthy subjects, and both the simulated and real-data experiments are mainly based on normal waveforms. For clinically more important abnormal or distorted waveforms, such as arrhythmias, conduction abnormalities, or ischemia-related changes, no targeted validation is provided. Therefore, it remains unclear whether the proposed denoising method may distort, attenuate, or overly smooth diagnostically meaningful pathological features. This limitation directly affects the credibility of the method for clinical application. Although the authors acknowledge in the conclusion that the method has only been validated on healthy subjects and that its ability to preserve pathological features remains unverified, I believe this issue is more than a general limitation; it is a fundamental weakness that significantly undermines the external validity of the paper’s conclusions. 7) The statement in the abstract that “The resultant equivalent noise floor on in vivo data reaches 6±6 fT/√Hz at 1 Hz on the real dataset—comparable to clinical-grade SQUID and OPM systems” should be treated with caution. This wording may easily give the impression that the system performance in this work is already close to that of clinical-grade SQUID/OPM systems, but whether such a claim is fully justified requires much more rigorous explanation. Although the manuscript mentions that the residual noise level is obtained “by converting SSD to noise PSD at 1 Hz following [17],” the paper does not provide sufficiently clear details regarding the calculation procedure, underlying assumptions, or physical interpretation. Considering that real magnetic noise is typically dominated by pronounced 1/f characteristics, and that thermal noise, environmental noise, and system noise have a much more complex composition, directly converting denoising error into an equivalent noise level and then comparing it to the intrinsic sensitivity floor of SQUID/OPM systems may be somewhat overstated. The authors should clearly explain the precise definition of this metric, the conversion procedure, the spectral assumptions involved, and its relationship to the true sensor noise floor, in order to avoid potentially misleading statements. author_feedback: We thank the meta-reviewer and all reviewers. We address all concerns below and will incorporate clarifications into the revision. Reviewer 1 Q1:Lack of pathological data Due to the lack of publicly available pathological TMR-MCG datasets, experiments are conducted on healthy subjects only. Evaluation on patient cohorts is planned as future work. Q2:Fusion interpretability The time-varying gate $A_\ell$ produces per-timestep branch weights where $A_{\ell,2}$ is consistently higher around QRS complexes and lower during baseline segments. We will add a heatmap visualization in the revision. Q3:Presentation All formatting issues will be corrected in the final version. Reviewer 2 Q1:Cycle-averaging as ground truth As described in [7], cycle-averaging is standard practice in TMR-MCG signal acquisition. If DFuse learned a smoothed template, it would not outperform all baselines trained with the identical reference. The gap over the second-best method demonstrates genuine signal recovery. Q2:Simulation realism PTB-XL waveforms are injected into a Helmholtz coil platform replicating the TMR sensor array and analog front-end, with noise directly acquired by TMR hardware. The simulated dataset therefore contains true signal labels (original waveforms before noise injection) and authentic TMR noise, validating two capabilities: whether DFuse learns global structured patterns rather than fitting arbitrary noise, and whether it suppresses TMR-specific noise while preserving morphology. Q3:Missing baselines We have conducted additional comparisons with SSP and MGU-Net and will include these results in the revision. Q4:Reproducibility Key details: MSE loss, AdamW, batch size 16, Caputo orders ${0.3,0.5,0.7,1.0}$. Full implementation details, code, and datasets will be released upon acceptance. Q5 follows R1 Q3. Reviewer 3 Q1:Writing Writing and terminology issues will be corrected throughout the revision. Q2:Novelty and motivation The unifying motivation of DFuse is spatially heterogeneous SNR across TMR-MCG channels: sensors close to the cardiac source capture high-amplitude signals while distant sensors are noise-dominated. A single encoder cannot simultaneously serve both regimes, inevitably trading off between structural coherence and local morphological detail. This directly motivates the dual-branch design: the Context-Aware Encoder provides a global rhythm scaffold robust to SNR variation, while the Morphology-Aware Encoder preserves fine-grained waveform transitions most at risk in low-SNR channels. Caputo fractional derivatives are chosen here because they are the only differentiable operator family continuously interpolating between trend integration and sharp transition detection via $\alpha$; Having two branches then naturally raises the question of how to combine them: different channels and cardiac phases require different feature mixes, motivating the time-varying and sample-wise gates in the Enhanced Fusion Block. CCR in the decoder closes the loop by leveraging reliable high-SNR channels to guide reconstruction of weaker ones. The ablation in Table2 confirms each component is necessary. Q3:Missing baselines The dominant noise in TMR-MCG is intrinsic 1/f and thermal sensor noise rather than environmental interference. SSS and tSSS assume spatial array completeness incompatible with our 5$\times$5 grid. We have conducted additional comparisons with SSP and MGU-Net and will report these results in the revision. Q4 and Q5 follow R2 Q4.Q6 follows R1 Q1.Q7:Noise floor claim Following [17], SSD is first converted to RMS noise in the time domain, then mapped to PSD by accounting for effective bandwidth, enabling direct comparison with sensor noise specifications in pT/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$. This estimates residual denoising error in field units rather than intrinsic sensor sensitivity. A derivation will be included and abstract wording revised accordingly.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their insightful feedback. We appreciate that the reviewers recognized the strong motivation of ECG-CoCa (R1), its meaningful technical contributions (R1, R3), the core representation modules (R2), and the comprehensive multi-task evaluation (R1, R3). We are also grateful for their recognition of our clear methodology, well-written presentation, and practical utility (R1, R3). We will release all code and datasets upon publication to ensure reproducibility and benefit the community. R1(1,2,3): Text Augmentation. Original ECG reports are often short and repetitive, leading to semantic collapse in contrastive learning. Text augmentation only adds objective physiological descriptors extracted from the ECG itself, without introducing extra diagnostic labels, thereby enriching supervision while preserving clinical consistency. For a fair comparison, all baseline methods were trained on the same augmented dataset, ensuring that the improvements stem from ECG-CoCa. Motivated by the reviewer’s suggestion, we further evaluated frozen ECG features via linear probing. ECG-CoCa achieves SOTA performance and remains competitive even without text augmentation. We appreciate this insightful advice and will consider more comprehensive representation-level analyses in future work. R1(4,5): Details of Implementation. Following prior works such as MERL and ECG-Chat, zero-shot prompts and the CCAR vocabulary are derived from standardized ECG diagnostic terminology, using clinically equivalent synonyms to reduce abbreviation ambiguity. For CCAR, clinical concepts are extracted by matching normalized report text to a predefined ECG concept vocabulary. These concept frequencies are then used to compute rarity-aware sample weights for generative training. R1(6): Morphology Module. Following common practice in MLLM alignment stage, the morphology module is frozen during Stage 2 to preserve stable features and prevent feature drift. Unfreezing it led to a 5% drop in zero-shot ACC, indicating that freezing this module is critical for maintaining robust and transferable ECG representations. R2(1): Novelty and Effectiveness of ECG-CoCa. ECG-CoCa is not a simple combination of contrastive and generative learning, but a unified framework that jointly models ECG representation, cross-modal alignment, and report generation. Unlike CLIP-style methods focusing on global alignment, ECG-CoCa preserves fine-grained morphology and rhythm dependencies via PI-DGE. In contrast to generative models such as HeartLLM, our CCAR and DCM further mitigate long-tail bias and semantic drift. Consistent improvements across Tables 1–3 further support the effectiveness of this unified design. R1(4)&R2(2,3): Details of Training Data. All compared methods were trained on the same datasets and identical patient-level/official splits to avoid data leakage, ensuring that the gains arise from the proposed architecture rather than additional training data. R3(1): Interpretability. We validated the learned representations through linear probing on PTB-XL, where the features showed clear separability for both morphology- and rhythm-related categories, supporting the physiological relevance of the proposed dual-granularity representations. We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion on more qualitative interpretability analyses and will consider additional visualizations and case studies in future work. R3(2,3): Training Objectives and Efficiency. We separately evaluated contrastive-only, generative-only, and joint training. The unified objective consistently achieved the best overall performance, indicating that contrastive and generative learning are complementary rather than merely additive. In terms of efficiency, joint training introduces only moderate overhead (~44 min/epoch) compared with contrastive-only (~30) and generative-only (~38). We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion and will consider more comprehensive analyses in future work.

Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The author’s response addresses the reviewers’ concerns. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The main weaknesses concern the evaluation protocol and the extent to which the reported gains can be attributed to the proposed model rather than to the enriched textual supervision and training setup. R1 raised a substantive concern that augmented ECG text may make retrieval and generation easier, and requested representation-level evaluation and ablations without text augmentation. The rebuttal clarifies that text augmentation uses objective physiological descriptors and states that baselines were trained under the same augmented-data setting. It also reports additional linear-probing and no-augmentation analyses. These clarifications reduce the concern, but the additional analyses are not part of the original submission and therefore cannot be treated as the primary basis for acceptance. The submitted paper would still benefit from a clearer description of prompt construction, clinical concept vocabulary construction, baseline retraining, and the exact role of augmented or template-based reports. R2 maintained a reject recommendation after rebuttal, mainly due to concern about unfair baseline comparison and possible data advantage. This concern was considered carefully. The rebuttal explicitly states that all compared methods were trained on the same datasets and identical patient-level or official splits. While this clarification is important, the original paper does not make the baseline retraining protocol sufficiently explicit, so some uncertainty remains. However, R2’s post-rebuttal justification focuses almost exclusively on this issue and does not fully engage with the broader methodological contributions, the submitted ablations, or the positive assessments from R1 and R3.Therefore, the remaining concern is considered a limitation of reporting and experimental transparency rather than a clear fatal flaw. R3 initially requested stronger evidence on the interaction between contrastive and generative learning, interpretability, and computational cost. The rebuttal addressed these points by clarifying separate training-objective comparisons and computational overhead. R3 judged these responses sufficient and maintained an accept recommendation. Some of these details should be added to the camera-ready version to improve reproducibility and transparency. Overall, the paper has meaningful methodological content, a relevant clinical signal-processing application, and a broad empirical evaluation. The novelty is not entirely radical, as the framework builds on established contrastive and generative paradigms, but the ECG-specific integration of dual-granularity raw-signal encoding, concept-aware generation, and diagnostic memory is sufficiently coherent and supported by results.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their thoughtful feedback and for recognizing the key strengths of our work: (1) the clinical relevance of predicting Echo-derived labels from the low-cost and easily accessible ECG, (2) the novelty of aligning ECGs with multi-view Echos, and (3) the comprehensive evaluation on multiple datasets and multiple downstream tasks. We now address the raised concerns: R1: OTiS as ECG encoder: We selected OTiS primarily for its computational efficiency: at 7.1M parameters, it is much more lightweight than ECG-specific alternatives such as ECGFounder (30.7M), xECG (57M), and ECG-FM (90.9M). Despite being a general time-series model, OTiS performs on par with these domain-specific alternatives on our downstream tasks (Table 3 & Figure 2). kNN classifier: We use kNN because it evaluates frozen embeddings directly without any parameter updates, providing a parameter-free measure of representation quality. This ensures that performance differences reflect embedding structure rather than classifier capacity. R2: Implementation details: Due to space constraints, training configurations are provided in our GitHub repository. Data processing is described in Section 4.1, and we refer the reader to the original OTiS and EchoPrime papers for further details. Echo view aggregation: The typical number of views per study can be derived from Table 1.To accommodate the variable number of views across studies, we pad studies to a uniform size (to the configured max. number of views per study=128) within each batch using zero-padding, and apply an attention mask during view aggregation to ensure padded views do not contribute to the resulting study embedding. Furthermore, our aggregation is permutation-invariant: since views within a study have no meaningful sequential order, the aggregator treats them as an unordered set, making the resulting embedding independent of the order in which views are presented. Retrieval threshold (±0.5 standard deviation): This threshold balances two considerations: (1) a single ECG is compatible with a range of structural phenotype values — which is precisely why we frame LVEF prediction as classification rather than regression — making exact matching overly strict and clinically unrealistic; and (2) thresholds beyond ±0.5 standard deviation produce too many chance-level correct matches, rendering Precision@1 uninformative. R3: Single-view vs. multi-view setting: Both settings use identical train/test data. In the single-view setting, each Echo view is treated as an independent sample, forming separate ECG↔view pairs (instead of ECG↔study pairs) without any aggregation module. No view selection heuristic is applied. At test time, in the single-view setting, the study-level embedding for retrieval is obtained by averaging individual view embeddings (as noted in Section 4.3). The key architectural difference from the multi-view setting is the absence of the view aggregator. Ethics and data compliance: Ethical approval, data access, and compliance details for our private institutional dataset will be included in the final manuscript. Pre-trained weights: We will release pre-trained weights in our GitHub repository.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for your constructive comments. We appreciate the recognition of our “motivated contribution”(R1&2), “methodologically novel design”(R1&2), and “reproducibility”(R1-3). Below we address general concerns followed by specific points. 1.Dataset representativeness and clinical translation(R1-3, AC). THINGS-EEG is a large-scale 82,160 trials and representative benchmark released by the THINGS initiative and leading institutions, and is widely used in EEG-to-image studies (ATM, UBP etc.). Healthy-subject data are not directly deployable to patients, so our work is claimed as algorithmic validation of stimulus-evoked EEG-to-visual-evidence decoding, as a first translation step before patient-specific calibration. Although DoC/CMD EEG introduces differences, healthy EEG also has large inter-subject variability; our results support robustness to variability, making the model promising for clinical transfer. CMD patients may retain stimulus processing without overt behavior, making behavioral assessment insufficient[1-4]. Decoded visual evidence from EEG signals can provide adjunct, clinician-reviewable support. We will add references and perform DoC/CMD validation in the future. 2.Experimental details(R2&R3). Retrieval is within-subject. Following published baselines, we report generation results on Subject 8 for fairness. Image conditions and RSVP are from THINGS-EEG acquisition protocol, not our task. We will clarify these points and further explain zero-shot N-way retrieval identification: N candidates include a true image and N-1 distractors, ranked by EEG-image embedding similarity. The 2-way metric is the N=2 case. Pixel-wise uncertainty is computed from 10 stochastic generations and can reflect both object reliability and structural stability. Unstable/failed generations make the object uncertain; structural drift affects background regions. From another perspective, the heatmap shows that Control Adapter reduces layout instability and thus better helps clinicians identify regions requiring caution. To R3, due to page limits, some details common in EEG-to-image studies are not fully restated. Gaining more related knowledge from [7] may be helpful for better understanding. 3.Task definition, readability and AI use(AC). Due to page limits, many abbreviations are used, we will remove them except MAMD and RFFA. EEG-to-image is not to visualize raw EEG traces, but to infer visual evidence from stimulus-evoked EEG: retrieval of the viewed image and reconstruction of a stimulus-consistent image. CLIP provides the visual embedding; diffusion synthesizes the image. AI was not used to generate or write the content but only for grammar/language polishing. 4.MAMD details. The batch dimension B is not changed. The permutation only follows PyTorch Transformer’s sequence-first convention. reviewer_2_strengths: The main contribution of the paper is the development of a deep learning model for Alzheimer’s detection using EEG data. However, the paper goes beyond just presenting the model: Uncertainty-Aware Learning: The model incorporates uncertainty estimation into deep learning, which enhances the reliability of predictions. This is especially important in healthcare, where having high confidence in the model’s output is critical. EEG Features for Alzheimer’s Diagnosis: The paper highlights the use of EEG-based biomarkers to detect Alzheimer’s disease, offering insights into how EEG signals can serve as a diagnostic tool. This is particularly valuable in the growing field of neuroimaging for disease diagnosis. Innovative Evaluation of Model Performance: The authors introduce new evaluation metrics to measure model performance in the context of uncertainty. They also discuss the model’s explainability, which is crucial when applying AI in medical settings. reviewer_2_weaknesses: Here are the main weaknesses of the paper: Clinical Validation is Lacking: While the paper presents a promising deep learning model for detecting Alzheimer’s using EEG data, it does not provide sufficient evidence of the model’s performance in real-world clinical settings. Clinical validation has been a key factor in similar studies like Rashid et al. (2021) and Gupta et al. (2019). Limited Comparison with Modern Approaches: The paper compares its model to traditional machine learning methods, but there’s no mention of how it fares against recent deep learning models, such as CNNs or RNNs, which have shown strong results in EEG-based medical diagnostics. Comparing with newer techniques, as seen in papers like Liu et al. (2020) and Zhou et al. (2021), would make the paper’s contribution clearer and more impactful. Overfitting Concerns: The results presented in the paper are promising, but the model might be overfitting to the relatively small dataset. This is important, especially in medical AI applications, where generalizability is key. Interpretability is a significant challenge for AI models in healthcare, and papers like Carvalho et al.
