author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for high-quality reviews. Below we provide point-to-point responses to the comments. [R1] Single dataset We use CirCor DigiScope, the largest heart sound data. Crucially, it’s the only data providing phase and site-specific annotations required for evaluation. Robustness is verified via patient-level 5-fold cross-validation, preventing data leakage and ensuring generalizability. [R1] Novelty PAHNet distinguishes itself by structurally aligning with cardiac physiology and localizing murmur-related phases and sites using only patient-level supervision. This provides clinical interpretability by identifying where and when a murmur occurs, which is not achieved by prior hierarchical or attention-based methods. [R1] Patient-level supervision justification We provide quantitative validation of interpretability claims in Table2.Removing patient-level supervision (PPC loss, config2) degrades murmur detection, localization, site prediction, and phase classification performance. [R1/R3] Not the best in all criteria While two models yield higher Accuracy, PAHNet achieves SOTA results in Precision, F1, AUC, and AUPRC and second-best in Recall. These metrics are more representative in unbalanced datasets. [R2] Dataset description & Ethical approval We use publicly available CirCor DigiScope data (widely used in prior works). It comprises 942 patients, with a murmur distribution of 179 present, 695 absent, and 68 unknown. To prevent leakage, 5-fold cross validation is split at the patient level. As a secondary analysis of de-identified data, this study is exempt from additional ethical approval. We will add more dataset details in the final version. [R2] Explainability PAHNet is designed with intrinsic explainability. Unlike black-box models that require post-hoc explanation tools, our PAFF/SAPF modules ensure decision-making is explicitly grounded in cardiac phases and sites. Removing these modules (Table2) leads to a significant performance drop, suggesting that PAHNet captures physiologically meaningful features. [R3] Unclear supervision and interpretability claims Training uses only patient-level labels. Temporal and site-level annotations are used for evaluation only. [R3] Preprocessing details Phase segmentation followed the official dataset reference. We use 20-cycle consecutive cropping (randomized in training, first 20 in testing). Zero-padding and binary masking are applied to missing cycles or sites. [R3] Unjustified design choices in fusion modules Sigmoid allows concurrent high weights across sites, essential as murmurs often propagate across multiple sites simultaneously. Phase-level classifier functions as a content-based detector for identifying murmur-like phases. Transformer captures contextual dependencies across phases. [R3] Strong assumptions in supervision strategy Murmurs are associated with specific phases (systole/diastole) as they arise from abnormal blood flow turbulence. PPC loss leverages this prior to focus on diagnostic phases, enhancing robustness against noise. Ablation study confirms this boosts performance compared to unconstrained learning. [R3] Unclear evaluation protocol and potential data leakage Data splitting is performed at patient level to prevent leakage. To handle variable numbers of sites, we use zero-padding for missing sites and apply a masking mechanism to ensure that only available sites contribute to diagnosis. [R3] Fairness of baseline comparison is unclear All baselines were trained using hyperparameters specified in original papers and evaluated under the same data split. PAHNet demonstrated consistent improvements over all baselines across 5-fold cross-validation. [R3] Ablation study lacks fine-grained analysis While certain factors change together due to functional interdependencies (e.g., removing Phase-level classifier in config4 disables PPC loss), our 7 ablation settings isolate the modular impact of each major innovation (PPC loss, PAFF, SAPF).

title: Real-Time Prediction of Impending Severe Fetal Distress Using Deep Learning on Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring
reviewer_1_strengths: The main strength of the paper is the use of a large multicenter dataset, including more than 18000 patients from multiple hospitals. This is an important aspect, as it increases the diversity of the data and supports the potential generalization of the model. Also is really important to have a dataset such as the one that this paper is proposing. The model produces a continuous risk score over time, which allows the evolution of the prediction to be analyzed. This is relevant from a clinical perspective, because it can help to monitor changes in fetal condition instead of providing only a single binary decision. The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The study focuses on antepartum fetal monitoring, while much of the existing literature on CTG-based prediction is focused on intrapartum data. A more explicit discussion of this difference, including the specific challenges and implications of antepartum prediction, would help to better position the contribution. The manuscript does not clearly describe the input data. It is not explicitly stated that the signals correspond to cardiotocography (CTG), including fetal heart rate and uterine contractions. This lack of clarity makes the methodology difficult to follow. The development and internal validation data are described as coming from the “NIA (AI-Hub) fetal monitoring dataset”, but no reference or description of this dataset is provided. It is unclear whether this is a public dataset or a proprietary one. Severe fetal distress is defined based on visual patterns in the same signals used as input, annotated by a limited number of clinicians. Given the known subjectivity and variability in CTG interpretation, this raises concerns about label reliability. This limitation is only briefly mentioned and deserves a more detailed discussion. The model is trained using a single 5-minute window per patient. For abnormal cases, the window is selected immediately before the event, while for normal cases it is randomly selected from the recording. This creates an asymmetry between classes and does not reflect the progressive nature of fetal compromise. As a result, the model may learn to distinguish late-stage patterns from randomly sampled segments, rather than learning to predict the evolution toward distress. The duration of the CTG recordings is not specified. This information is important to understand how much temporal context is available and to better interpret the 5-minute window strategy. The manuscript reports an “optimal threshold” (0.294) in the figures, but the origin of this value is not clearly explained. The use of a large multicenter dataset with external validation is a strength, but similar large-scale studies have been reported in the literature, especially in intrapartum CTG analysis. The use of both fetal heart rate and uterine contraction signals reflects standard clinical practice and is not a novel aspect. The proposed 5-minute prediction window is also not clearly justified. The manuscript presents UMAP visualizations and Grad-CAM analysis, but these methods are not clearly introduced or explained. In particular, the UMAP projections do not show a clear separation between normal and abnormal cases, and the conclusions drawn from these visualizations are not sufficiently supported. This part of the analysis is difficult to interpret. Some claims in the discussion are not supported by evidence. The manuscript suggests that a 5-minute prediction window would enable effective preventive interventions. However, this claim is not supported by references.

Sec. 2.2 specifies that “the 5-minute window immediately preceding the event was extracted” for abnormal cases, while for normal controls “one 5-minute window was randomly selected.” We gently note that external validation does not rely on this 1:1 sampling: “the remaining continuous record was segmented into 5-minute windows, excluding a washout period” (Sec. 2.2), yielding 183,016 continuous windows simulating real-world monitoring. title: Riemannian Batch Normalization on Correlation Manifolds for EEG Decoding
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Well-defined and technically sound problem formulation The paper identifies a clear gap: existing batch normalization methods cannot be directly applied to correlation matrices due to the unit-diagonal constraint defining a strict submanifold. Addressing normalization on this specific manifold is a meaningful and well-motivated problem in Riemannian deep learning for EEG. 2.Principled geometric design leveraging Lie group structure CorBN is carefully derived using the Lie group structure of the correlation manifold under the Off-Log Metric. The method performs centering via Fréchet mean, scaling in the tangent space, and biasing through group action, providing a geometrically consistent analogue of Euclidean batch normalization. This principled formulation is both mathematically elegant and conceptually clear. 3.Closed-form and computationally efficient implementation Unlike some Riemannian normalization approaches that rely on iterative procedures (e. g. , Karcher mean), CorBN admits closed-form expressions for its key operations. This improves computational efficiency and makes the method more practical for integration into deep learning pipelines. 4.Theoretical justification of statistical behavior on manifolds The paper provides a statistical interpretation of CorBN through Riemannian Gaussian distributions, showing how the method controls mean and variance on the manifold. This strengthens the contribution beyond a heuristic design and connects it to established probabilistic principles. 5.Consistent improvements and improved training stability Experimental results across multiple EEG benchmarks demonstrate consistent performance gains and reduced variance. Additionally, training dynamics analysis shows faster convergence and more stable gradients, which aligns with the intended purpose of normalization layers.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Limited methodological novelty relative to prior work While CorBN is well-formulated, it is conceptually an extension of existing normalization techniques to a specific manifold. Riemannian batch normalization for SPD matrices has already been introduced, and Lie group-based normalization methods have also been explored. The main contribution here is adapting these ideas to the correlation manifold under the Off-Log Metric, which is a meaningful but incremental extension rather than a fundamentally new paradigm. 2.Modest empirical improvements The reported performance gains are relatively small (typically around 0.5 ~ 1% across tasks), as shown in the comparison tables. While consistent, these improvements are limited in magnitude and may fall within the variability of training, raising questions about the practical impact of the method in real-world applications. 3.Limited experimental scope and dataset diversity The evaluation is conducted on a small number of standard EEG benchmarks (e. g. , BCIC-IV-2a, MAMEM-SSVEP-II, ERN), which are relatively small and commonly used datasets. There is no validation on larger-scale or more clinically relevant datasets, which limits the generalizability and real-world applicability of the findings. 4.Lack of strong comparisons with recent state-of-the-art methods Although several baselines are included, the comparison does not fully cover the most recent advances in EEG decoding or manifold-based deep learning. In particular, newer architectures or normalization techniques are not extensively benchmarked, which weakens the claim of state-of-the-art performance. 5.Limited ablation and sensitivity analysis The paper provides some ablation on the placement of CorBN layers, but lacks deeper analysis of key design choices. For example, there is no exploration of sensitivity to the chosen metric (e. g. , Off-Log vs. alternatives), the effect of scale and bias parameters, or comparisons with simpler normalization strategies. This makes it difficult to fully understand the contribution of each component. 6.Weak clinical relevance and application impact Although EEG is mentioned as a clinical modality, the paper focuses on standard decoding tasks (e. g. , motor imagery, SSVEP, ERN) rather than clinically meaningful outcomes. There is no demonstration of clinical feasibility, diagnostic utility, or integration into medical workflows, which limits its impact for application-oriented venues such as MICCAI.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for the very constructive comments. 1.@R1@AC: Novelty. CorBN is related to prior Riemannian/Lie-group normalization, but is not a direct transfer of existing BN. Correlation matrices form a strict SPD submanifold with a unit-diagonal constraint; thus Euclidean or SPD-based BN may violate valid Correlation geometry. Moreover, BN operations, including centering, scaling, biasing, and running-statistics updates, are metric- and manifold-dependent. Under OLM, they must be re-derived using the specific Lie group structure, where the logarithmic map lies in the hollow symmetric space and the exponential map requires diagonal correction to preserve unit diagonals. CorBN thus provides a missing normalization primitive for Correlation-valued neural networks. It defines OLM-consistent batch statistics, centers samples by group translation, controls dispersion in the OLM tangent space, and applies learnable bias while preserving the manifold constraint. This is important for EEG decoding, where Correlation matrices capture scale-invariant inter-channel dependencies beyond covariance-based SPD descriptors. CorBN also benefits from closed-form OLM-related operators and trivialization-based optimization [NeurIPS, 2019], making it a practical step toward deep learning on Correlation manifolds. 2.@R1@R2@AC: Accuracy. However, EEG decoding is noisy and subject-dependent, where consistent improvements are non-trivial. CorBN improves stability, reducing standard deviations from 2.78 / 3.22 / 3.40 to 1.98 / 2.82 / 3.27.Compared with SPDNetBN, CorBN achieves larger gains of +2.47%, +5.62%, and +7.25%. Subject-level paired Wilcoxon tests further support significance over CorAtt: MI (p=0.0039), SSVEP (p=0.0059), and ERN (p=0.000214). 3.@R1@AC: Dataset. We additionally evaluate CorBN on TUAB, a clinical abnormal-EEG benchmark [Frontiers in Neuroscience, 2016] with over 400K EEG samples. We also compare with LaBraM-base, a recent EEG foundation model [ICLR, 2024], which reports 0.9022±0.0009 AUROC. Under the same setting, LaBraM-base+SPDNetBN obtains 0.9034±0.0021, while LaBraM-base+CorBN achieves 0.9098±0.0011.These show CorBN remains effective on a larger clinical dataset and works as a pluggable module that can be compatible with large EEG model. 4.@R1: Ablations. We add component-wise ablations on the three used datasets. Centering alone achieves 75.01±1.68 / 68.09±2.73 / 75.57±3.63, Centering+Scaling improves to 75.12±2.49 / 68.24±3.00 / 75.70±3.54, while Full CorBN: Centering+Scaling+Bias, obtains the best accuracy. These show that each component contributes and the learnable bias helps restore a task-adaptive manifold mean after normalization. 5.@R1: Metric choice. OLM is not arbitrary. It is a permutation-invariant log-Euclidean geometry designed for Correlation matrices [SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl., 2024]. Its Riemannian operators naturally support CorBN computations while preserving the unit-diagonal constraint. In contrast, LSM involves the log-scaling bijection and diagonal matrix-scaling, making the BN pipeline less direct. We choose OLM for its simpler and implementation-friendly geometry, and will add detailed analysis in the revision. 6.@R1@R2: Reproducibility. Once accepted, we will release all the implementation codes and files on GitHub as soon as possible. 7.@R2: Limitations. CorBN is designed for scenarios where scale-invariant inter-channel dependency is discriminative. It may be less effective when absolute magnitude, channel variance, or covariance energy carries task-relevant information, since Correlation representations remove scale information. On the RADAR dataset, where covariance magnitude reflect target reflection intensity, motion strength, distance attenuation, and signal energy, SPDNetBN outperforms CorAtt-BN (94.85±0.99 vs 93.89±2.11). This suggests CorBN is not universally preferable and seems to be more beneficial for EEG-like signals dominated by dependency pattern.

Thus, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewer concerns seem to have been addressed adequately in the rebuttal response. Overall, the paper appears to offer a good balance between methodological novelty, appropriateness for the application, and empirical justification. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes CorBN, a Riemannian batch normalization framework designed for correlation manifolds to improve EEG decoding while preserving the geometric constraints of full-rank correlation matrices. The work addresses a clear methodological gap by introducing a geometrically principled and computationally practical normalization layer that is tailored to correlation-valued representations, with a sound theoretical formulation and consistent empirical improvements across multiple EEG decoding tasks. While the contribution is somewhat incremental relative to prior Riemannian and Lie-group normalization methods and the performance gains are modest, the rebuttal sufficiently clarified the manifold-specific necessity of the approach, strengthened the empirical justification through additional analysis, and discussed limitations more clearly. Excluding the additional TUAB evaluation results introduced in the rebuttal and basing this assessment on the submitted paper together with rebuttal clarifications, I find that the main concerns are sufficiently mitigated. Overall, the work is technically solid, well motivated, and provides a useful normalization primitive for correlation-manifold learning.

title: S-CEReBrO: Breaking the Memory Barrier in Continuous EEG Monitoring
reviewer_1_strengths: One of the most compelling strengths of the paper is its clear focus on a real and pressing systems-level problem: the incompatibility of Transformer architectures with continuous, long-duration EEG monitoring. Rather than proposing incremental performance improvements on short benchmarks, the authors tackle a constraint that directly limits real-world deployment. This grounding in practical constraints significantly strengthens the contribution. The proposed Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism is a well-motivated and carefully designed solution to this problem. While locality-based attention has been explored in other domains, the specific formulation here, which combines temporal and spatial windowing with alternating layers, dilation, and shifting, demonstrates a thoughtful adaptation to the unique structure of EEG data. The mechanism balances efficiency and expressivity by maintaining local attention while still enabling indirect long-range interactions through layer-wise propagation. The additional design choice of enforcing constant KV memory through explicit token eviction further distinguishes the approach from many prior efficient attention methods. Another notable strength is the integration of algorithmic innovation with system-level design. The use of streaming via FIFO buffering is not merely an implementation detail but a core part of the model’s functionality. This allows S-CEReBrO to operate continuously without artificial segmentation, preserving temporal coherence in a way that many prior approaches do not. The accompanying scaling experiments provide convincing evidence of the practical benefits, showing substantial improvements in both memory usage and inference speed, as well as the ability to handle significantly longer signals. The experimental evaluation is broad and comprehensive, covering 11 downstream tasks that span clinical, cognitive, and BCI applications. This diversity strengthens the claim that the learned representations are generalizable. Moreover, the model achieves state-of-the-art performance on 7 of these tasks despite having a relatively small parameter count. This highlights an important insight: that carefully designed inductive biases and efficient attention mechanisms can outperform larger models relying on global attention. The paper also benefits from large-scale pretraining on a diverse EEG corpus, which is essential for foundation model performance. The inclusion of heterogeneous datasets with varying channel configurations and recording conditions supports robustness and generalization, and the use of masked autoencoding aligns with successful strategies in related domains. Finally, the work offers an implicit but important conceptual contribution: it challenges the assumption that global attention is necessary for high-quality EEG modeling. By demonstrating strong performance with localized attention, the paper suggests that exploiting the inherent spatiotemporal structure of EEG signals may be more effective than relying on fully global interactions.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Despite its strengths, the paper’s novelty is somewhat limited when viewed in the broader context of efficient Transformer research. Many of the core ideas underlying the proposed method, such as windowed attention, locality constraints, and separating spatial and temporal attention—have been explored in prior work. For example, sliding window attention has been used in models like Longformer, and alternating spatial-temporal attention is already present in the original CEReBrO architecture. As a result, the primary contribution lies more in the combination and adaptation of existing ideas rather than the introduction of a fundamentally new mechanism. While this integration is well executed, the paper could more clearly articulate what aspects are truly novel and why they are uniquely suited to EEG. Another limitation is the lack of comparison with a broader set of long-context attention methods. The evaluation focuses on a subset of EEG foundation models and baselines, but omits several influential approaches from the efficient attention literature, such as Performer or Longformer-style architectures. Without these comparisons, it is difficult to determine whether the observed gains are specific to the proposed design or simply reflect the general advantages of locality and reduced memory usage. The paper would also benefit from more extensive ablation studies. Key components of the model, such as window sizes, dilation factors, and the alternating structure, are introduced without a detailed analysis of their individual contributions. This makes it challenging to assess which elements are essential and whether simpler variants could achieve similar performance. In particular, understanding the trade-offs between window size and performance would be valuable, especially given the central role of locality in the model. A related concern is the limited investigation of long-range dependency modeling. While the authors argue that long-range interactions can be captured indirectly through the alternating attention structure, this claim is not rigorously validated. There is little analysis of scenarios where global context might be important, nor any controlled experiments demonstrating the model’s ability to capture dependencies over long time horizons. This leaves open the question of whether the efficiency gains come at the cost of missing important temporal relationships. From an empirical standpoint, although the model achieves state-of-the-art results on several tasks, the performance improvements are not uniformly strong. In some cases, the gains over existing methods are modest, and on at least one task the model underperforms simpler baselines. This suggests that the benefits of the proposed approach may be task-dependent, and the paper could provide a more nuanced discussion of where and why the model excels. Finally, there are some reproducibility concerns. Certain references are anonymized or incomplete, and the paper provides limited details about training procedures, hyperparameter tuning, and implementation specifics. The absence of code or a clear statement about availability further complicates the ability of others to validate and build upon the work.

reviewer_2_strengths: Novel windowing (temporal and spatial/cross-channel) technique for handling streaming data in a trasformer-like architecture for multi-channel signals (such as EEG). reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Precise Problem Formulation with Practical Significance: The linear growth of KV cache with signal length in continuous EEG monitoring is a real engineering bottleneck. This paper is the first work to reduce the resident memory of EEG foundation models to O(1). The comparison in Table 1 clearly demonstrates this unique advantage. 2.Elegant Design of Windowed Alternating Attention: The combination of alternating attention (existing work) with windowed locality (from LLM domain), adapted to EEG’s 2D spatiotemporal structure via dilation/shift factors (rather than simply transplanting 1D text window attention), is a clear and targeted design. Replacing fixed segmentation with FIFO streaming maintains temporal continuity, which is crucial for scenarios like seizure detection. 3.Extremely Comprehensive Experiments: 11 downstream tasks cover clinical (seizure detection, sleep staging, abnormal classification), BCI (motor imagery, emotion recognition), and cognitive monitoring (workload, alertness), spanning 128-1000Hz sampling rates, 6-64 channels, and 4-30s durations. Reporting mean ± standard deviation of 5 random seeds for all results demonstrates excellent statistical rigor. 4.Compelling Scaling Analysis: Fig. 2 clearly illustrates the advantages of windowed alternating attention in memory and inference latency—it can process 30,000s (8h) signals, which is 60× longer than full self-attention and 2× longer than linear attention. It also uses 2.8× less memory and is 3.7× faster in inference. 5.Outstanding Parameter Efficiency: With only 2.4M parameters, it is the smallest among all foundation model baselines (BIOT 3.2M, CBraMod 4.0M, LaBraM 5.8M), yet performs better on most tasks. This is not only an academic contribution but also has significant value for practical deployment. 6.Thoughtful Ablation Design: The supplementary CEReBrO paper includes attention mechanism comparison (Table V), channel embedding strategy comparison (Table VI), pretraining effects (Table VII), and quantization analysis (Fig. 3), clearly attributing contributions to each component. The direct comparison of S-CEReBrO vs CEReBrO in Table 5 proves the additional gains of the windowed mechanism’s local inductive bias in cognitive monitoring tasks. 7.Complete Empirical Evidence for MCU Deployment: The deployment validation on GAP9 with 350ms latency and 10mJ energy consumption verifies a complete closed loop from theory to practice, which is first-of-its-kind in the EEG foundation model domain.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Insufficient Discussion on Losing Long-Range Dependencies: The paper claims “global attention is often redundant for EEG analysis,” yet S-CEReBrO did not reach SOTA on 4 tasks (SHU-MI, TUAB, ISRUC, Mental Arithmetic). Notably, the gap is significant on Mental Arithmetic (68.97% vs best 75.66%). The paper does not analyze whether these tasks require global temporal dependencies or the limitations of the windowed mechanism in these specific scenarios. 2.Lack of Systematic Analysis on Window Size Selection: wt=5 and ws=7 are fixed hyperparameters, but the paper lacks sensitivity analysis for different window sizes. The optimal window size may vary across tasks and sampling rates. The rationale for choosing dilation factors {1,2, 4} and shift factors {0,1, -1, 2, -2} is also not explained. 3.Insufficient Analysis of Data Distribution Differences: Pretraining is dominated by TUEG clinical data, but downstream tasks include BCI and emotion recognition, which are significantly different. The paper does not analyze how the domain gap affects the performance of different tasks.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their feedback. We itemise our responses. 1) Distinction from Longformer, Performer, & FIFO. EEG decoding is bidirectional: tasks generally require past+future context around each prediction. WAA’s core property is that the active-token neighborhood is bounded by design: every query at (c,t) attends only to N_t and N_s (Eq. 3,5) independently of T. The KV cache only holds tokens inside these neighborhoods, yielding O(1) memory. FIFO implements this: as new tokens stream in, those outside every future query’s neighborhood are evicted. Information from evicted tokens is preserved through depth, because WSA mixes channels at each timestep before eviction, and alternating WSA/WTA layers propagate features forward (Sec. 3.2-3). Competing methods lack both space-time prior and O(1) KV cache memory under bidirectional inference: Longformer’s 1D windows break EEG structure, and the bidirectional form needs an O(T) KV cache. Performer uses content-agnostic random features with no spatial/temporal prior, and its bidirectional kernel sum materializes the entire sequence (O(T)). WAA is the only mechanism combining O(1) KV memory with an EEG-aware spatiotemporal prior under bidirectional decoding (Table 1). 2) Long-range dependencies & benchmark scope. Current EEG datasets operate on second-scale segments; minute/hour-scale labeled benchmarks are not publicly established. Our paper shows that locality can improve performance: S-CEReBrO leads at long and short segments alike: CHB-MIT (10s), SEED-VIG (8s), Neonate (5s), STEW (4s) (Table 4). The scaling claim (Fig. 2) is a capability result: WAA is the only mechanism running at hour-scale, so no baseline comparison is currently possible. Establishing such benchmarks is important future work our architecture enables. 3) Non-SOTA tasks & window/dilation rationale. A single configuration across tasks is a core goal; per-task tuning would contradict the foundation model premise. w_s=7 covers standard 10/20 montage neighborhoods and w_t=5 is the smallest window whose cascaded receptive field over the 3 WTA layers covers the 30s pre-training context; shifts {0,±1,±2} tile contiguous receptive fields across dilations {1,2,4} without gaps (Sec. 3.2-3.3, Table 2). Of the 4 non-leading tasks, TUAB (−0.06 AUROC vs CBraMod), ISRUC (−0.70 F1 vs CBraMod) and Mumtaz (−0.78 AUROC vs BIOT) are within one std. Mental Arithmetic shows the largest gap (6.69 AUROC), but its 1,707 samples are an order of magnitude smaller than other benchmarks and the leader is a small supervised model, indicating sample efficiency rather than receptive field is the bottleneck. We respectfully note that R3 lists SHU-MI as non-leading, but S-CEReBrO leads SHU-MI (66.48 vs BIOT 66.16). 4) Reproducibility. All datasets are public and cited. Anonymized reference [2] is our prior work under review at a different venue. We detail the architecture and hyperparameters in our manuscript and will release code upon publication. 5) Difference from CEReBrO. CEReBrO uses global alternating attention with O(T) resident memory (Table 1), making 8-hour streaming infeasible. S-CEReBrO introduces bounded space-time neighborhoods, achieving O(1) KV cache and 6× longer signal capacity (Sec 3.4,Fig. 2). This is an architectural change, not tuning. S-CEReBrO’s gains over CEReBrO are notable (Table 5): on STEW +3.14% Balanced Acc, +3.10% Weighted F1, +0.0213 Cohen κ; on SEED-VIG, -0.0114 RMSE and +0.0209 Pearson. 6) Pre-training/downstream domain gap. We analyze how the gap affects each task in Table 4.Grouping tasks by distance from TUEG: clinical tasks close to TUEG (TUAB, Mumtaz, CHB-MIT) yield leads or within-std results; BCI tasks (PhysioNet-MI, SHU-MI) yield leads or within-std results; affective/state tasks (SEED-V, SEED-VIG, STEW) all lead; the pediatric task (Neonate) leads. S-CEReBrO retains performance on distant tasks. This robustness comes from the channel embeddings (Sec. 3.1), which handle different montages.

In the final revisions It is recommended to add structural definitions of the bounded space-time neighborhoods and the mathematical constraints yielding the cache are added in Section 3, also add discussion on the limitation of the sample starved dataset. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Two reviewers independently assigned the high score (5) and R2 maintained this after reading the rebuttal. The rebuttal convincingly distinguished WAA from Longformer (O(T) KV cache under bidirectional decoding, incompatible with EEG spatial structure) and Performer (content-agnostic, O(T) materialization), addressing the sole dissenter’s main concern about novelty. The O(1) KV cache achievement -the O(1) memory result is practically important for the field-, SOTA on 7/11 tasks with “only” 2.4M parameters, large-scale pretraining on 25k hours of diverse EEG, and MCU deployment validation form a comprehensive and practically significant package. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers raised concerns regarding the novelty of the proposed attention mechanism, the ability of the model to capture long-range dependencies, the rationale behind the selected windowing parameters, and the limited comparison with other efficient attention architectures. The rebuttal addressed these concerns satisfactorily by clarifying the FIFO streaming mechanism, the bounded space-time neighborhood design, the relationship to existing efficient attention methods, and the rationale for the selected window and dilation configurations. The paper addresses an important practical limitation of current EEG foundation models by enabling continuous long-duration monitoring with constant KV-cache memory requirements. The proposed architecture demonstrates strong scalability characteristics while maintaining competitive or state-of-the-art performance across a broad set of downstream tasks. Although questions regarding extremely long-range temporal dependencies remain valid limitations, the current experimental evidence supports the effectiveness of the proposed design for realistic EEG monitoring scenarios.

title: SA-CFM: Structure-Aware Continuous Flow Matching for Normative Modeling of EEG Microstate
reviewer_1_strengths: In my view, the major strength of the paper is to introduce a framework of normative modeling with flow matching. Diagnosis and subtyping with the gap between reconstructed features from flow matching are interesting.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The comparison baselines seem not to be very comprehensive. For example, what about the performance of conditional diffusion models? What about microstate features + strong classifiers (XGBoost / Transformer et al. ; The method of “Raw features” in Table 2 is not described in detail)?
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The case against stochastic normative models is principled and correct. VAE posterior sampling introduces irreducible variance into deviation scores, and using a deterministic flow is a well-motivated solution. The evaluation is methodologically rigorous: two independent PD cohorts, strictly subject-independent 5-fold MCCV with fixed seeds — rare in EEG-based neuroimaging. The ablation is clean; Table 4 shows each component contributing incrementally, with the full model consistently outperforming all ablations across both cohorts. The interpretability analysis holds up: the dissociation between transition-specific discriminability (Trans_A_D, Trans_A_C) and global entropic signatures is a biologically meaningful finding, not post-hoc decoration. Training exclusively on 1,419 healthy controls with no disease labels is the correct normative paradigm. And the near-chance performance of end-to-end EEG classifiers is reported honestly and used to justify the normative framing, which strengthens rather than undermines the argument.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1- AEPD has only N=32 patients! the second independent cohort on which the generalization claim partly rests. Under 5-fold MCCV, some folds have fewer than 7 test subjects. The standard deviations are large (±6.48%), and the reported 88.6% subject-level accuracy on this cohort is unreliable. Conclusions drawn from AEPD should be heavily caveated. 2- The normative training data is heterogeneous and unharmonized. The 1,419 healthy controls span age 17–88 across five datasets with different acquisition protocols. EEG microstate statistics are acquisition-sensitive, and pooling without site correction could introduce systematic biases into the normative reference. 3- The KAN-VAE downstream head is unjustified. A VAE is used as the classification head on top of the flow matching normative model, reintroducing stochastic sampling at the exact stage the paper argues against. The justification ( that a VAE induces a structured latent space for clustering ) is weak and directly contradicts the central argument for deterministic reproducibility. 4- Only age is conditioned on. Sex, education, medication status, and disease duration (all known confounds in PD cognitive research ) are ignored. This is a significant limitation that goes undiscussed. 5- No reproducibility analysis is reported. The central empirical claim is deterministic reproducibility over VAE stochastic inference — yet no quantitative comparison of run-to-run deviation score variance between SA-CFM and cVAE is provided. This is the most important claim in the paper and it is supported only theoretically.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1) The paper is very well written 2) The exploration of microstates constitutes both the primary novelty and the core strength of this paper. 3) The framework is feature-agnostic and inherently stable.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for the constructive comments. We focus on the key concerns raised in the meta-review and reviews. [AC/Meta] We address the main concerns identified in the meta-review: reproducibility, baseline fairness, evaluation completeness, cohort size, data heterogeneity, and methodological details. [R1] Baselines and fairness. cVAE is the direct stochastic conditional-generative baseline for testing deterministic normative inference; a conditional DDPM would also be stochastic and would not directly test deterministic inversion. Microstate+XGBoost/Transformer classifiers test supervised discriminative learning rather than normative deviation modeling. Our controlled comparison fixes the 27-D input and the same KAN-VAE head for GAMLSS, cVAE, and SA-CFM, isolating deviation encoding. “Raw Features” in Table 2 means k-means directly on the 27-D vector, a non-normative lower bound. [R1] Channel layout and microstate computation. All datasets were standardized to the common 19-channel 10-20 montage; for recordings with more channels, only these shared 19 channels were retained. The model consumes 27-D microstate statistics, not channel-indexed signals. GFP-peak k-means (k=4, 10 restarts) is followed by spatial-correlation matching to canonical A-D templates on this shared montage; statistics are computed in this fixed order. No hierarchical clustering is used. [R1] Low end-to-end EEG accuracy. Inputs were z-scored per channel per subject. Under subject-independent splits, the near-chance results of five end-to-end baselines in Table 3 suggest that direct segment-level discrimination is unstable under strong inter-subject heterogeneity, motivating normative deviation modeling. [R2] Reproducibility of deviation scores. We distinguish inference determinism from training randomness. For a fixed trained SA-CFM model and fixed-step RK4 solver, backward ODE integration maps each input to one unique latent deviation representation; no posterior sampling is involved. In contrast, cVAE inference uses a posterior distribution and, even with the 10-MC averaging in Sec. 3.2, retains sampling-induced variance. Table 2 reports clustering stability under the same downstream head: SA-CFM ARI = 0.58/0.65 vs cVAE 0.33/0.39.[R2] AEPD size and generalization. We agree that AEPD (N=32) should be read as a secondary independent-cohort test, not the sole basis for generalization. The primary evidence is PD-RS (N=100) under subject-independent 5-fold MCCV with 5 fixed seeds, and AEPD uncertainty is reported transparently. The claim rests on cross-cohort consistency: Subj-Acc 83.0%/88.6%, deltaMoCA 3.32/3.96, and ARI 0.58/0.65.[R2] Heterogeneous normative data. All training cohorts used the same pipeline (128 Hz, 0.5-45 Hz filtering, ADJUST-ICA, GFP-peak k-means). We use 27-D microstate temporal/transition statistics rather than channel-indexed raw signals, and condition on age, the dominant covariate available in all cohorts. Fig. 2(a) shows a smooth unimodal latent norm distribution with PD-RS HCs overlapping the normative range, suggesting no gross site-separated structure. [R2] KAN-VAE and determinism. The deterministic claim concerns the normative deviation representation before any downstream head. KAN-VAE is applied identically to GAMLSS, cVAE, and SA-CFM, so its stochasticity is controlled and does not alter SA-CFM inversion in Eq. 5.Table 4 shows SA-CFM without KAN already improves over naive/attention CFM; KAN is an additional shared nonlinear readout. [R2] Single-covariate conditioning. Age is the only covariate uniformly available across all six datasets. Sex, education, and medication are missing in several training cohorts; including them would shrink or bias the normative reference. Disease duration cannot be used for a model trained exclusively on healthy controls. We hope these clarifications address the reviewers’ and AC’s major concerns.

title: ShapeEFM: A Shape-Based Pretrained Foundation Model on ECG Morphology Comprehension
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The motivation of this work is clear and well-grounded. The paper identifies that existing ECG self-supervised methods stress rhythm or high-level semantics while underrepresenting continuous waveform morphology, making the shape-oriented re-design of representations genuinely heuristic. 2.The technical pipeline is complete, forming a coherent flow from morphological unit construction, tokenizer training, vocabulary learning, to masked pretraining. 3.The approach carries certain interpretability, transforming ECG signals into finer-grained linguistic units with ablation experiments and latent space visualizations offering preliminary support for representation learning effectiveness.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The boundary of key innovation remains insufficiently defined. The proposed framework closely resembles existing ECG language modeling methods such as HeartLang. At the high-level framework, the primary change appears to substitute heartbeat-level tokenization with PIP-based turning point segmentation, suggesting novelty lies more in segmentation granularity and representational units rather than the pretraining framework itself. 2.The claim of overcoming discrete segmentation limitations appears overstated. The proposed method still relies on explicit segmentation and discretization, merely employing finer-grained morphological segmentation rather than fixed windows or heartbeat cuts, rather than escaping discrete segmentation per se. 3.The robustness of the segmentation strategy requires thorough validation. As HeartLang noted, prior fine-grained segmentation methods suffer from signal quality sensitivity, and even QRS-Tokenizers struggle with irregular QRS complexes and baseline drift. ShapeEFM’s PIP algorithm operates at finer granularity with extreme dependence on local waveform turning points, rendering it more vulnerable to baseline drift, high-frequency noise, and muscle artifacts. Since subsequent Cardio-Morpheme construction, vocabulary learning, and prediction targets all rest upon segmentation quality, boundary instability may undermine entire pretraining reliability, yet the paper currently provides only basic filtering without direct segmentation robustness or noise sensitivity analysis. 4.The generalization from single-lead segmentation to 12-lead settings lacks sufficient justification. The paper explicitly states that PIP discovery executes only on Lead I, then applies the resulting keypoints across all 12 leads. This embeds a strong assumption that Lead I morphological boundaries adequately represent local morphological variations across all leads. However, different leads reflect identical cardiac electrical activity projected along different spatial directions, with local waveform morphology and turning point positions not necessarily strictly consistent. The paper offers no dedicated analysis of this assumption, nor comparison experiments with per-lead segmentation or multi-lead joint segmentation, leaving this design’s rationality inadequately explained. 5.Experimental evaluation depth should be expanded. Current experiments rely primarily on linear probing, ablation studies, and qualitative visualization. This work lacks cross-dataset generalization analysis, systematic robustness testing, and statistical significance testing, rendering existing experiments more indicative of potential than establishing significant advantages over existing methods. 6.Method description and experimental settings could be clarified to guarantee reproducibility. For instance, pretraining data MIMIC-IV-ECG and downstream data EchoNext, CSN exhibit inconsistent sampling frequencies, while the method employs fixed hyperparameters closely related to the temporal scale, such as PIP quantity ratios and maximum Cardio-Morpheme length. The paper fails to clearly clarify whether different sampling rates underwent unified resampling, or how these hyperparameters maintain comparability across different temporal resolutions. 7.In the method section, some reused symbols suffer from inconsistency issues, increasing comprehension and reproduction costs.

author_feedback: AC/R1/R2/R3: This response addresses key clarifications regarding method novelty, PIP segmentation robustness, the rationale for Lead-I-only segmentation, implementation details, statistical significance, and clinical interpretability. We revised the manuscript to make ShapeEFM’s novelty boundary clearer. HeartLang and ShapeEFM both use ECG language modeling, but with different levels of tokenization and self-supervised reconstruction targets. Unlike HeartLang, which compresses each beat into one word and largely relies on the accurate detection of the QRS complex, ShapeEFM treats sub-beat morphology changes such as QRS widening and ST deviation as reconstruction units, making these clinically relevant transitions explicit targets of SSL rather than implicit within heartbeat tokens. And these morphology-level shapelets enhance model’s representation capability for ECG morphology. Our PIP extraction algorithm relies on local waveform to reduce baseline drift’s effect, and we employ a low-pass filter to mitigate high-frequency noise. In addition, the codebook learned in the VQ step helps absorb subject-specific muscle artifacts after segmentation. Internal validation on the full MIMIC cohort using synthetic noise (±0.5mV baseline drift; 20-100Hz EMG) reveals that mean PIP location deviation was 1.2ms (less than 10% of the 16ms Cardio-Morpheme scale), supporting its stability under these perturbations. Our choice of Lead-I-only PIP segmentation leverages Lead I’s higher SNR relative to precordial leads, and provides a shared temporal scaffold for synchronized 12-lead ECGs. This strategy not only enhances robustness but also yields better performance: our internal ablation study comparing two segmentation strategies revealed that Lead-I-only segmentation achieved an AUROC (CSN 100%) of 89.80%, surpassing the 88.45% obtained by the multi-lead approach. For implementation, polyphase filtering is used to upsample EchoNext data from 250 Hz to 500 Hz, aligning it with pretraining frequency. ShapeEFM consists of 12 Transformer encoder blocks, 8 attention heads, and a dropout rate of 0.1, which is added to the manuscript. We commit to release the full codebase upon paper acceptance to facilitate reproducibility. We also conducted repeated experiments with 5 random seeds, and employed paired t-test to confirm ShapeEFM’s improvements are statistically significant. Notably, these gains are robust in multiple scenarios, including low-data regimes (CSN 10% AUROC: p=0.008) and full-supervision settings (EchoNext 100% AUROC: p=0.003). The statistical analysis have been incorporated into the revised Table 2.For clinical interpretability, we divided patients into ST-depression (>0.5mm) and normal groups, clustered the Cardio-Morpheme vocabulary into 12 categories, and analyzed distribution differences via the Chi-Square Test (p<0.05). Results indicate that the most significant cluster linked to ST-depression exhibits negative slopes or reduced amplitudes compared to normal levels (updated in revised Fig 3). R1: We agree that our segmentation wording was too strong. ShapeEFM does not eliminate discrete segmentation, it mitigates fixed-window/heartbeat-level tokenization limits through adaptive morphology-aware segmentation. We have softened this claim in the manuscript. For Cardio-Morpheme configurations, both the PIP count and maximum length are fixed when the signal duration and sampling frequency are constant. We apply upsampling to accommodate inconsistent frequencies. We also fixed the symbol reuse issues. R2: The association between specific clusters and ST-depression has been detailed in the preceding section. Regarding the suggestion to overlay model attention on clinically relevant segments, we agree this is also valuable and plan to pursue it as future work. R3: The similarity to HeartLang is addressed above by clarifying the different morphology-level tokenization design and SSL reconstruction target. We fixed the Fig. 3 label error
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I recommend an Invite for Rebuttal. The reviewers praised the paper’s clear motivation to capture continuous ECG waveform morphology, the completeness of the technical pipeline, and the strong downstream empirical results on the EchoNext and CSN datasets. However, several critical technical and methodological concerns must be addressed. First, the authors must clarify the boundary of their key innovation, as reviewers noted the framework heavily resembles existing models like HeartLang, with the primary difference being the segmentation granularity rather than a fundamental departure from discrete segmentation. Second, the authors need to rigorously validate the robustness of the PIP-based segmentation algorithm against baseline drift, high-frequency noise, and muscle artifacts, while also justifying the strong assumption of applying Lead I’s segmentation boundaries across all 12 leads. Third, the rebuttal must supply missing implementation details, specifically regarding how inconsistent sampling frequencies across pretraining and downstream datasets were handled, the training setups, and the number of transformer encoders used. Furthermore, the authors must report statistical significance tests (e.g., p-values) for their performance improvements to ensure the reported gains over baselines are robust. Finally, the authors should deepen the clinical interpretability analysis by correlating learned features with established clinical markers, correct the mislabeled ST segment in Figure 3, and fix any inconsistent mathematical symbols in the methodology section. | The paper introduces an ECG foundation model that captures sub-beat waveform morphology, and the authors’ comprehensive rebuttal effectively resolved initial concerns by clarifying the method’s novelty over existing baselines, proving the segmentation’s robustness to noise, and providing necessary statistical significance tests. Although one reviewer ultimately felt the methodological novelty remained limited, the thorough empirical validation, proven downstream performance, and the newly added clinical interpretability analyses linking learned features to ST-depression justify its acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The motivation is clear and important, while the empirical gains are incremental against strong baselines, and the evaluation is limited to linear probing on two downstream datasets, so the “foundation model” framing is somewhat stronger than the demonstrated transfer scope. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Thank you for the detailed rebuttal. We appreciate your time and effort. The rebuttal successfully addressed the main concerns raised during review. The authors clarified the novelty relative to prior ECG language models, repositioning ShapeEFM as a morphology-aware tokenization and reconstruction framework rather than a departure from discrete segmentation. Additional evidence on segmentation robustness, Lead-I design choices, implementation details, statistical significance, and clinical interpretability substantially strengthened the submission. Although the novelty remains incremental and further clinical discussion would improve the work, the contribution is technically sound, reproducible, and supported by stronger experimental evidence. I recommend to Accept this paper.

author_feedback: We respectfully thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We address the concerns below in a consolidated manner, grouping related issues across reviewers. [Clarity] (R1-W1,W2): SiLU(x)=x·σ(x) (Elfwing et al., 2018); will be added in Eq.(2). Training details (weighted CE, AdamW lr=1e-3, cosine annealing, early stopping, surrogate gradient) will be consolidated in the revision. [Statistical Robustness] (R2-W1,W2): We performed 10-run bootstrap resampling on all models and report mean±std. For example, SpikeMamba-L on PTB achieves 91.72±0.39% vs Medformer 83.50%. The full mean±std results were omitted due to page limits and will be included in the revision. [State-Dependent Gate Ablation] (R3-W1): We ablated the gate by comparing SpikeMamba-L with and without the State-Dependent Gate across three datasets: ADFTD (53.62% vs 53.22% Acc), PTB (91.72% vs 90.79% Acc), PTB-XL (74.16% vs 73.97% Acc). The gated variant consistently outperforms by selectively suppressing redundant spikes during inactive segments. [Hyperparameter Sensitivity Ablation] (R2-W1,W2; R3-W1,W4): All gate parameters (κ, δ, λ₁, λ₂, τ_g) are learnable and adapt during training. We swept V_th ∈ {0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0} and κ ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.45, 0.5} on PTB-Medium. V_th=1.0 yields the best accuracy (89.00%) and F1 (92.27%); performance degrades symmetrically for lower/higher values. κ ∈ [0.01, 0.3] maintains stable accuracy (87.98–89.07%). Increasing κ reveals the gate’s energy–accuracy trade-off: at κ=0.5, energy drops to 22.11 mJ, a 39.5% reduction vs. the no-gate baseline (36.55 mJ) at the cost of 4.07% accuracy and 2.91% F1.At κ=0.45, energy is 23.65 mJ with only 2.61% accuracy and 2.26% F1 trade-off, demonstrating the gate as a controllable energy–performance knob beyond core LIF dynamics. These results will be included in the revision. [Baseline Comparisons] (R2-W4; R3-W2): We include parameter-matched Vanilla Mamba (8L-404D, ~8.6M params) as a direct non-spiking baseline across all five datasets. At identical parameter count, SpikeMamba-L outperforms Vanilla Mamba on PTB (91.72% vs 89.16%) and matches on PTB-XL (74.16% vs 74.23%). On CHB-MIT, SpikeMamba-L achieves substantially higher seizure sensitivity (89.15% vs 71.26%). Across all datasets, SpikeMamba consumes 30–40× less energy (e.g., 322.91 vs 12,184.98 mJ on PTB). For Table 3, we evaluated iTransformer, MTST, and Reformer on CHB-MIT and MIT-BIH. On CHB-MIT, iTransformer and MTST failed to detect seizures (sensitivity 0% and F1≈0%). Reformer achieved 80.26% accuracy with 78.21% sensitivity, but SpikeMamba-M outperformed it in accuracy (88.57%), F1 (80.02%), and AUROC (94.48% vs 88.19%) at 10.5× lower energy (56.86 vs 598.41 mJ). On MIT-BIH, all models achieved comparable accuracy (98.46–99.02%), with SpikeMamba-M consuming 5.6–44.8× less energy. These results will be included in the revised manuscript. [EEG Data Split] (R2-W3): CHB-MIT uses segment-level split (6:2:2) as few seizure events per subject make subject-wise splitting impractical. PTB, PTB-XL, and ADFTD use subject-independent splits following Medformer. [ADFTD & Non-Spike Phenomena] (R1-W4; R2-W5): Medformer’s F1 advantage on ADFTD (50.65% vs 46.58%) reflects its cross-resolution routing for heterogeneous EEG patterns. SpikeMamba-L matches accuracy (53.62% vs 53.27%) at 44× lower energy (262 vs 11,590 mJ). The LIF neuron operates in latent space; depthwise convolutions and learnable leak coefficient α capture cross-channel and non-spike temporal dynamics. [Hardware & Future Work] (R2-Future; R3-W3): Current energy estimates are theoretical. We plan deployment on MindCore which is an FPGA-based neuromorphic hardware system to validate real-world energy/latency. Remaining suggestions will be addressed in the revised Future Work section. [Reproducibility] (R1,R2,R3): Full source code, hyper-parameters, and preprocessing scripts will be released upon acceptance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Please prioritize clarifying the method and training procedure, including the temporal spike encoder, SiLU definition, loss function, and optimization details. Additionally, address concerns about experimental rigor, especially subject-wise splitting and possible EEG leakage, cross-validation or statistical significance, missing baselines such as vanilla Mamba, and inconsistent baseline comparisons across tables. | The paper proposes SpikeMamba, a computationally efficient state-space model for time-series biosignals that avoids continuous dense updates and introduces new architectural components, including state-dependent gates. The proposed design is promising not only for biosignal analysis but also as a potentially extensible approach for other sequential modeling applications. A key strength of SpikeMamba is its substantial reduction in energy consumption, achieving several-fold improvements while maintaining competitive performance against more energy-intensive models across five datasets. During review, several concerns were raised regarding experimental rigor, method clarification, and training details. In the rebuttal, the authors provided a comprehensive response, clarifying important aspects including statistical robustness, state-dependent gate ablations, baseline comparisons, and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis. These clarifications were recognized by the reviewers, some of whom increased their scores and recommended acceptance. Overall, the paper presents a strong and practically relevant contribution, and is recommended for acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After considering the rebuttal and updated reviews, I recommend rejection. Although the paper addresses an important topic, reviewers still raised several substantial concerns after the rebuttal. In particular, some key issues would require additional experimental evidence that cannot be adequately resolved at this stage. Therefore, I do not think the paper meets the acceptance threshold. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes SpikeMamba, an event-driven state-space architecture for energy-efficient biomedical sequence modeling. The idea of integrating spiking dynamics with state-space modeling is interesting and relevant for resource-constrained biomedical monitoring. The submitted manuscript evaluates the method across five ECG and EEG benchmarks and reports competitive predictive performance together with substantial theoretical energy reductions. The reviewers raised valid concerns regarding the completeness of baseline comparisons, the lack of dedicated ablation for the state-dependent gate, and the theoretical nature of the energy evaluation. Nevertheless, the rebuttal clarifies the training setup and provides a reasonable response to the major concerns. Overall, I consider the work novel and promising enough for acceptance, while recognizing that the experimental validation could be strengthened in future work.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank the AC and Reviewers for constructive feedback and for recognizing the novelty of our SAIR framework. (Q-question A-additional comment) 1.ATS Accuracy Mismatch (R2A11) We clarify that the ATS paper’s main table reports results from a single seed (seed=0), as evidenced by their accuracies ending in 0.5% (200-way) and confirmed in their supplementary material. For rigorous evaluation, we report the average performance across 5 runs (seeds 0-4). Our reproduced 5-seed average for ATS (58.1%) closely aligns with the only overall 5-seed average provided in their supplementary material (59.07%). 2.Comparison with NeuroBridge (R2Q2) NeuroBridge is an excellent concurrent work. Since it was officially published online in Proceedings of AAAI on 16 March 2026, it was not included as a baseline. We acknowledge their inter-subject advantage (19% vs. 17%). However, our paradigms differ fundamentally: NeuroBridge simulates cognitive-level perceptual variability via statistical data augmentation (e.g., noise, mosaic), while SAIR extracts structural features (Edge, Depth, Foveal) related to the early visual system for structurally constrained alignment. We view these two contemporaneous works as highly complementary, and exploring the fusion of SAIR with NeuroBridge would be an exciting future direction. 3.Component Novelty (R1A2&A3) We deliberately utilized standard GAT and InfoNCE for stable feature extraction and fair benchmarking. Our core novelty lies not in inventing components, but in the system-level SAIR framework. By uniquely integrating biological structural cues into a multi-embedding contrastive paradigm, we provide a novel solution to the visual-EEG semantic mismatch problem. 4.Topology-agnostic Mode Stability (R2A7) We honestly acknowledge that discarding GAT in cross-subject settings is an engineering compromise to prevent overfitting to subject-specific spatial artifacts, as stated in Sec. 2.3.In our work, model stability relies on the robust shared representation space established by CLIP, which warrants further investigation and improvement in future work. 5.Foveal Blurring on Off-center Objects (R2A5&R3Q1) Things-EEG was collected using the standard Rapid Serial Visual Presentation paradigm, where a central fixation cross continuously guides the subjects’ attention to the screen center. Thus, under this protocol, central blurring is an accurate biological reflection rather than a limitation. We will explicitly detail this to resolve ambiguity. Extending our work to free-viewing settings is a direction for future work. 6.Computation Trade-off (R1A2) We acknowledge that the three embeddings triple the resource requirements. Moreover, since the three branches compute in parallel, actual inference latency remains low. 7.Independent λ Weights (R2A8) Independent tuning of λ weights in Eq. 3 yielded only marginal gains over equal weighting. We chose equal weights to prioritize simplicity. 8.Training Details & Reproducibility (R1A3) Our core training configurations are already detailed in Section 3.We apologize if they were easily overlooked. It is not demonstrated why this architecture can effectively separate subject-specific and task-specific features. author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers and the meta-reviewer for their valuable feedback. We address each concern below, grouped by topic. 1.Novelty (R1.2). While contrastive learning and meta-learning have been used in EEG analysis, existing studies have focused on a single task/dataset setting, without considering generalizability. Moreover, current EEG foundation models solely rely on self-supervised learning without leveraging semantic information. Our contribution lies in leveraging semantic information for EEG foundation model to learn more generalizable EEG representations. 2.Disentanglement (R1.3, R2.1, R2.4, R2.7, R2.8, R3.2). Disentanglement itself is not new in EEG analysis. We adopt the design of [3], but our novelty lies in being the first to integrate disentanglement into an EEG foundation model trained across multiple tasks/datasets via meta-learning, boosting performance and generalizability. For R2’s concerns, all variants in Table 4 show statistically significant improvements (p<0.05). The t-SNE on ISRUC demonstrates that task-dependent features form class-wise clusters across subjects, while subject-dependent features are well separated regardless of class. 3.Comparison (R1.1, R3.1, R3.7, R3.8). We followed the same experimental settings as previous works. Reproducibility issues have been reported on the official baseline GitHub repos; thus, we reproduced baselines with a large gap using official code. EEG-DINO was reproduced as it was not validated on our settings. For R1 and R3’s concerns, the gaps over baselines are statistically significant (p<0.05). We will state this, soften SOTA to consistent improvements, and clarify that some scores come from reproducing with official code. 4.Evaluation scope (R1.5, R2.6, R3.6). We agree that broader validation would further strengthen the work. Notably, we found that STEM also shows similar performance trends on the Mumtaz dataset, supporting the generalizability. 5.Missing baselines (R3.3). Existing EEG meta-learning methods focus on formulating each subject as an individual task to mitigate inter-subject variability, and target single-task few-shot scenarios. In contrast, STEM leverages multiple task labels alongside subject IDs via meta-learning. Due to these different setups, direct comparison is not entirely straightforward. We will clarify these differences in the revised paper. 6.Corrections (R3.5). The correct scores were AUCPR = 0.5231 and AUROC = 0.5827.7.Related work (R2.2, R3.4). We primarily focused on EEG foundation models due to space limitations. We will expand it to cover related studies suggested by R2 and R3.Importantly, while prior works have been conducted on a single task/dataset, our work extends these to a multi-task/dataset setting. 3D-coordinate encoding is not intended as a primary contribution, but rather shares a similar purpose to the related approaches mentioned by R3.8.Additional ablations (R1.4, R2.3, R2.5, R3.9). Pretraining takes ~2 weeks, making ablations such as scalability, loss weights, scaling law, and design choices difficult to complete within the rebuttal period. However, regarding (R2.3) and (R2.5), we verified the effect of loss weights and the scale of training samples during fine-tuning. For (R2.3), task loss weight showed larger variance than subject loss weight, and deviating from the default values led to performance degradation, particularly when weights exceeded 1, as they interfere with the primary objective. For (R2.5), STEM achieves comparable results to the baselines even when fine-tuned with half of the training samples, suggesting the effectiveness of meta-learning in enabling data-efficient fine-tuning. Regarding (R1.4), STEM requires significantly fewer MACs than EEG-DINO, though more than others due to 5× more patches from our smaller patch size. We believe this can be improved through exploration of optimal patch sizes. We agree these analyses would strengthen the work and will discuss them.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a subject- and task-aware EEG foundation model that integrates semantic supervision with contrastive self-supervised learning and meta-learning. The motivation is well aligned with challenges in EEG representation learning, particularly inter-subject variability and task heterogeneity. The method is evaluated across multiple datasets and includes few-shot adaptation experiments, which are relevant and valuable contributions. The reviewers raised several concerns regarding the positioning and validation of the contribution. In particular, the claim of state-of-the-art performance appears overstated, as the reported results are not consistently stronger than existing methods under comparable evaluation protocols. The novelty of the disentanglement mechanism is also partially incremental, with related prior work not sufficiently discussed or differentiated. Also, some inconsistencies in reported results and experimental details further reduce confidence in the claims. However, the core idea is promising, and the paper presents a meaningful direction by combining semantic supervision with foundation model pretraining. The concerns raised primarily relate to positioning, validation, and clarity rather than fundamental flaws. Given the above, the paper is invited for rebuttal. The authors are encouraged to: -Clarify benchmarking protocols and moderate claims of state-of-the-art performance. -Strengthen comparison with relevant prior work, particularly in disentanglement and meta-learning. -Include additional baselines or justify their absence. -Provide statistical validation such as variance and significance testing. -Resolve inconsistencies in reported results. | The rebuttal addressed the major concerns reasonably well by clarifying that the main contribution is the integration of semantic supervision and meta-learning within a multi-task EEG foundation model setting, rather than proposing disentanglement itself as a novel concept. The authors also clarified benchmarking details, corrected inconsistencies in the reported results, and addressed the absence of statistical significance reporting. While some limitations remain, particularly regarding broader validation and deeper theoretical analysis, I believe the major concerns were sufficiently addressed and the paper is above the acceptance threshold. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have sufficiently addressed the major concerns from the reviewers. EEG foundation models can an interesting topic for the MICCAI community. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have addressed most of the concerns raised by the reviewers.

title: Test-Time Adaptation for ECG Classification via SQI-Gated Self-training and Beat-Rhythm Consistency
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper is generally well organized and clearly presents the proposed framework, with Fig. 2 effectively illustrating the overall pipeline and workflow. 2.The motivation is well introduced. The authors show that generic TTA methods are suboptimal for ECG classification because they are sensitive to noisy signals and do not capture ECG-specific beat-rhythm semantics. To address these gaps, the paper proposes an ECG-tailored adaptation framework for more reliable cross-domain classification.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The performance gains are consistent, but the absolute improvements remain relatively modest. For example, in the offline setting, the average Macro-F1 increases from 60.64% to 62.42%, and Macro-AUC from 88.13% to 88.84%. The paper would be stronger if the authors could better contextualize the practical significance of these gains, particularly with respect to their potential clinical relevance. 2.While the results on the two target datasets provide a useful starting point, the experimental scope remains relatively narrow. Restricting evaluation to a shared 6-class label space substantially simplifies the adaptation problem compared with real-world ECG diagnosis. To better support the paper’s claims of practical utility, the authors should provide a more thorough discussion of how the proposed method may generalize to broader diagnostic categories and more diverse clinical settings beyond the current evaluation.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses an important issue. Domain shift is a practical problem that directly affects the usability of models in clinical applications. It applies the TTA to a relevant domain and proposes the use of meaningful features aligned with application (e.g., beat structure and rhythm-level). The incorporation of SQI into TTA to handle noise is a practical and efficient design choice. The experimental setup and execution appear adequate, with evaluations across different settings and comparisons against a diverse set of methods from the literature. The use of multiple datasets is appropriate for assessing domain shift. The evaluation includes different scenarios (offline, continual online, and independent online). The structure and organization of the paper are clear and easy to follow.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Although the ideas are relevant and coherent, the level of innovation does not constitute a major methodological advance. The method mainly provides incremental improvements through a combination of established techniques, with novelty relying more on their application to TTA rather than on fundamentally new concepts. The reported performance gains are modest. The paper lacks statistical significance testing and confidence intervals across models and settings. While improvements appear consistent, they are relatively small. Additional evaluation metrics (e.g., balanced accuracy or sensitivity) would be valuable, especially given their importance in clinical contexts. Although the ablation study demonstrates the contribution of each module, the paper lacks deeper analysis. In particular, there is no per-class performance evaluation, qualitative examples comparing methods, and no discussion of how the improvements translate into clinical settings. The discussion section is relatively superficial. The paper does not sufficiently analyze failure cases or conditions under which drift affects performance. Additionally, without confidence intervals, the robustness of the method under different scenarios remains unclear. Some implementation details are missing or insufficiently described. These include augmentation strategies, certain model parameters, and aspects of the loss formulation. The SQI thresholds are not fully justified. Although code is provided, it is not straightforward to follow due to limited documentation. All key details affecting reproducibility should be clearly described in the paper itself.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The proposed method is evaluated in publicly available standardized datasets in three protocols - offline, continual online and independent online and compared with state-of-the art methods.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The performance comparison between the proposed method and existing state-of-the-art techniques is inherently biased. Specifically, the authors adopted the optimization strategy of disabling dropout and updating only BatchNorm affine parameters which was derived from [17] for their own method and SAR [17]. Omitting this strategy for the remaining baselines results in an unfair evaluation framework. [17].
