author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and ACs for the constructive comments. We are encouraged that reviewers recognized the clinical motivation, ECG-specific design, and clear organization of our work. We are committed to revising our manuscript accordingly and address the main concerns below. 1.Fairness of adaptation settings (R4). We thank R4 for noting this ambiguity. The manuscript described the update scope of our method, which may have implied that this setting was applied only to our method and SAR. This is a presentation issue, not an experimental bias. All methods used the same source checkpoint, target stream, preprocessing, and protocol-specific adaptation budget, while following their official/default implementation protocol. We used no privileged dropout or extra trainable parameters compared to baselines. We will explicitly list the dropout handling and adaptation scope of each baseline. 2.Per-class performance (R2/R5). Due to page limits, we did not include the full per-class table, but we examined class-wise performance. Under independent online TTA setting, compared with SAR, our method improves IAVB/LBBB/RBBB/PAC/NSR F1 from 62.48/68.97/85.95/10.06/52.78 to 67.57/70.32/86.22/14.39/54.91, while AF slightly decreases from 83.72 to 82.40.Thus, the gain is not driven by a single class but we will avoid claiming uniform per-class improvement. 3.Statistical testing (R2). To quantify the consistency of observed improvements (averaged over three runs), we performed paired t-tests against the strongest baseline per protocol. The resulting p-values for Macro-F1 are p=1.356e-05, p=7.216e-05, and p=3.911e-03 for offline, continual online, and independent online TTA. Macro-AUC improvements are smaller and will be interpreted cautiously. 4.Robustness under degraded signals and R-peak dependence (R5). We additionally tested ECGs degraded by Gaussian noise and baseline wander. In offline TTA, Ours achieves Avg AUC/F1 88.64/60.89, outperforming UCon 88.06/59.97 and Source Only 88.03/59.38.In independent online TTA, Ours achieves 88.07/59.54, compared with SAR 87.82/58.04 and Source Only 87.77/57.81.This suggests SQI-gated adaptation remains stable under common waveform degradations. While this cannot fully isolate R-peak errors, future work will examine detector choices, peak detection errors, and noise severities. 5.Limited evaluation scope and generalizability (R1/R5). We agree that clinical ECG diagnosis covers more conditions. Using PTB-XL (source) and CPSC2018/Georgia (targets) provides a controlled cohort and acquisition shift setting. The shared 6-class space is required for closed-set TTA and enables fair comparison across datasets with inconsistent diagnostic taxonomies. Handling unseen classes is an open-set problem beyond current scope. Future work will explore unknown-class rejection and broader label spaces. 6.SQI design, thresholds, and implementation details (R2/R5). SQI is a lightweight unsupervised reliability gate for updates, not a clinically validated quality classifier. It reflects general ECG waveform properties: QRS energy concentration, QRS sharpness, and baseline-wander suppression. After robust normalization, these dimensionless terms are combined as a soft gate to down-weight unreliable samples. The thresholds tau_c=0.2 and tau_q=0.05 are fixed across all target datasets/protocols without target-label tuning. We will also specify the strong-view augmentations: Gaussian noise, gain jitter, and one temporal mean-mask, without time shift, crop, or warping to preserve beat-window alignment. 7.Modest absolute gains and contribution (R1/R2/R5). The gains should be viewed in the difficult label-free, source-free TTA setting, where avoiding model collapse during online updates is challenging. Our framework yields consistent improvements across each protocol by suppressing artifact-driven updates via SQI gating. We will emphasize this deployment robustness while avoiding overstatement.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes an ECG-tailored Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) framework utilizing SQI-gated self-training and beat-rhythm consistency. While reviewers appreciate the modality-specific clinical motivation, the consensus leans borderline due to concerns regarding evaluation fairness, statistical rigor, and edge-case robustness. Specifically: -R4’s concern regarding biased optimization settings (BatchNorm/dropout updates) applied to your method versus the baselines. -per-class performance breakdowns (R2, R5). -Analyze the framework’s sensitivity to R-peak detection failures under severe noise or domain shifts (R5). -Justify the limited evaluation scope (2 target datasets, shared 6-class space) and discuss generalizability (R1). | This paper presents a clinically well-motivated test-time adaptation framework tailored to ECG multi-label classification, which effectively integrates physiological structure via SQI gating and dual-level consistency. Although concerns regarding baseline optimization fairness and modest absolute gains were raised, the authors’ post-rebuttal clarifications, additional statistical tests, and noise-degradation experiments successfully satisfied the majority of the review panel. Balancing the methodological suitability for clinical deployment against the remaining minor baseline ambiguities, a Weak Accept is recommended. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After reviewing the manuscript, the reviews, and the authors’ rebuttal, I recommend acceptance. The rebuttal adequately addresses most of the major concerns raised during review. In particular, the additional analyses, statistical testing, and degraded-signal experiments strengthen the empirical evidence supporting the proposed approach. This is reflected in the updated assessments from Reviewers 1 and 5. I acknowledge the remaining concerns regarding the interpretation of certain design choices and the limited evaluation scope. However, these issues do not undermine the core contribution or the validity of the reported results. Overall, I believe the paper makes a solid contribution and that the remaining weaknesses are not sufficient to outweigh its strengths. Therefore, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): I would lean toward rejection. Although the paper addresses a relevant ECG test-time adaptation problem and the proposed SQI-gated beat/rhythm consistency design is reasonable, the contribution appears incremental and the reported gains are relatively modest. More importantly, several concerns remain insufficiently resolved, including the fairness of baseline comparisons, the heuristic SQI formulation, dependence on reliable R-peak detection, and the limited closed-set 6-class evaluation. Therefore, I am not fully convinced that the current evidence supports acceptance at MICCAI.

title: VEGA: Vision Enhanced Generative Augmentation for Cross-Subject Electrocardiogram Generalization
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper directly tackles a well-known challenge in ECG analysis: severe inter-subject variability that leads to poor generalization on testing patients. Instead of relying on traditional fine-tuning techniques, which may risk data leakage, VEGA solves the distribution gap from a data generation perspective. By enriching the training manifold with diverse, generated cross-subject samples, it forces the downstream networks to focus on task-relevant discriminative features rather than memorizing patient-specific backgrounds. The latent space visualization (Fig. 3) provides convincing evidence that VEGA effectively aligns the training and testing distributions. 2.The methodological highlight of this work is the highly creative cross-modal adaptation. Training high-fidelity generative models (such as Diffusion) from scratch typically requires massive amounts of ECG data, which is clinically impractical. VEGA elegantly bypasses this by exploiting the spatial/structural similarities between natural images and the periodic waveforms of ECGs. The strategy of dividing 1D ECGs into segments and stacking them column-wise into a 2D matrix successfully preserves both intra-cycle morphology and inter-cycle dynamics.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.While the authors position VEGA primarily as a generative augmentation framework, the empirical validation lacks comprehensive comparisons with existing time-series data augmentation techniques. In the generative heartbeat prediction task (Table 2), VEGA is only compared against NF and DDPM For the core clinical downstream tasks, the experiments only compare the baseline models against themselves with VEGA augmentation (i. e. , Model vs. Model + VEGA). Without more baselines, it is difficult to determine whether the performance gains are uniquely attributed to VEGA or merely the general benefit of having more training data. 2.The assumption of ‘label preservation’ during the generative augmentation process. The authors utilize a MAE that masks a certain proportion of the input and reconstructs it, claiming that ‘the original task labels are preserved for the generated outputs. However, this claim lacks validation. In cardiovascular diagnostics, diseases like VPB are often characterized by highly localized, subtle morphological anomalies. If the random masking mechanism happens to obscure these critical pathological regions, the MAE might utilize its learned priors to reconstruct a morphologically ‘normal’ waveform. Assigning the original pathological label to this smoothed or normalized reconstruction would inadvertently introduce noisy labels into the training set, potentially confusing the downstream classifier.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Strong few-shot efficiency results. Table 2 shows that VEGA with only 10% training data outperforms DDPM and normalizing flows. Task-agnostic design. VEGA is applied across multiple downstream architectures and distinct tasks without task-specific modification.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Missing baselines for the generative component and the adaptation component. The prior works (Chen et al. and Yoon et al.) are cited in related work but absent from comparison. The inference-time sampling procedure is not clearly described. It is ambiguous whether generation proceeds by masking a contiguous future segment of an existing training sample and reconstructing it, or by generating from scratch? The paper motivates 2D conversion, but providees no comparison against 1D-based generative baselines. Without this comparison. The paper repeatedly claims that VEGA produces “diverse” augmented samples, but provides no quantitative evidence of diversity.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper formulates the ECG reconstruction problem not as a purely end-to-end generation task, but as a structured problem leveraging ECG vector relationships. It introduces a hybrid strategy in which only one limb lead is reconstructed via learning, while the remaining limb leads are derived analytically using physiological equations. The proposed IGUANA framework combines a lead representation learner with an AdaIN-based 1D U-Net generator and incorporates both source reconstruction and representation consistency in the training process. Comprehensive experiments are conducted on both PTB-XL and CUSPH datasets, including comparisons with competing methods, claim validation, and loss ablation studies. The reconstructed 12-lead ECG achieves AUROC and AUPRC performance close to that of the original ECG in downstream disease prediction tasks.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The method largely resembles an integration of existing lead reconstruction architectures with ECG-based analytical relationships, and thus does not strongly highlight methodological novelty. The experimental setting fixes the input lead to Lead I and the auxiliary lead to Lead II, but lacks sufficient validation of generalization across different lead configurations. The rationale for adopting the current 6-to-6 conditioning scheme in precordial lead reconstruction is not sufficiently compared with alternative design choices. Since the proposed approach follows a staged reconstruction pipeline, further analysis is required to examine the potential accumulation of reconstruction errors across stages. Some competing methods rely on the authors’ own implementations, leaving potential bias due to differences in reproduction settings.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank AC and all reviewers for their efforts and constructive feedback. All your constructive comments are considered. 1.The novelty, integration concern and error accumulation (MR[3]) (1) Novelty of the Paradigm: VEGA is the first systematic framework that bridges visual priors and 1D ECG generation to enable cross-subject augmentation without data leakage. Its tailored frequency adapter freezes self-attention to preserve spatial priors learned from images, while explicitly injecting global spectral information to model ECG’s periodic nature. The design effectively disentangles spatial and spectral features, and its superiority is quantitatively validated in Table 2. (2) Integration Innovation: All model components are elaborately designed rather than arbitrarily assembled, forming a minimal yet indispensable architecture. Specifically, the MAE captures reconstructive visual priors, instance normalization enables amplitude bridging, frozen self-attention preserves pre-trained prior knowledge under limited data, and the Frequency Adapter achieves spectral alignment. Our contribution lies in the synergistic combination of these modules, instead of their isolated individual functions. (3) Error Accumulation Issue: Unlike conventional autoregression, VEGA adopts single-step parallel decoding for future ECG segments, thereby inherently avoiding long-horizon error accumulation—a deliberate architectural design to enhance model robustness. 2.Label preservation and inference-time sampling procedure (MR[2]/R1[2]/R2[2]) During inference, VEGA converts the ECG into a 2D representation and maps it to the left image half via bilinear interpolation without masking, so no information is lost. The right half is fully masked and reconstructed by the MAE. For augmentation, the alignment loss targets the original sequence; for prediction, it targets the future sequence. The substantial Recall and F1-score improvements after VEGA augmentation (Fig. 4) confirm that sensitivity to positive samples is preserved without distorting pathological waveforms. Predictive generation visualizations (Fig. 5) further verify that VEGA faithfully reconstructs key waveform morphologies under varying conditions. 3.Diversity issue (R2[4]) Regarding generation diversity, we provide both mechanistic explanations and visual evidence. (1) Source of diversity: Diversity is inherent in our design. First, bilinear interpolation during 2D resizing introduces sub-patch shifts (hyper-parameter η). Second, the MAE’s stochastic masking naturally produces varying outputs from the same input, since different visible patch mosaics yield distinct completions. (2) Latent space evidence (Fig. 3): Latent feature visualization shows that VEGA substantially broadens the training distribution toward the test set, directly evidencing the generation of diverse, subject-variant features that bridge the generalization gap. 4.Lack of comprehensive baselines (MR[1]/R1[1]/R2[3]/R2[1]) As clarified in Q1, VEGA is the first framework bridging visual priors and 1D ECG generation for cross-subject augmentation. It adopts a cross-modal paradigm of visual pre-training and fine-tuning on a small external ECG dataset. In contrast, diffusion models and normalizing flows typically require large amounts of data; fine-tuned on the same limited data as VEGA, they would suffer mode collapse, produce nearly pure noise, and cause a sharp performance drop. To demonstrate VEGA’s few-shot generative capability, we employ conditional generation (i.e., predictive generation), which effectively alleviates the mode collapse problem prevalent in diffusion and other mainstream methods. As Table 2 shows, VEGA achieves better generative performance with far fewer training samples than other 1D generative methods. In the revised version, we will rigorously add more baseline comparisons under fair experimental settings to validate the advantages of the proposed method.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): While reviewers agreed that the paper addresses important challenges in ECG analysis and features innovative design elements, they also raised serious concerns about the paper’s evaluation rigor, methodological clarity, and novelty: First, the empirical validation lacks comprehensive baselines, and relevant prior works are absent from comparisons, making it hard to attribute performance gains to the proposed methods. Second, key claims and procedures lack validation or clarity. Third, methodological novelty is not strongly highlighted, with one method resembling an integration of existing architectures and insufficient justification for design choices. Since the reviews are mixed, we would like to invite the authors to provide a rebuttal. In addition to clarify other concerns, please try to address the following points during rebuttal: include comprehensive comparisons with existing time-series augmentation techniques, 1D-based generative baselines, and relevant prior works; validate the “label preservation” claim and clarify the inference-time sampling procedure; highlight methodological novelty, justify key design choices, and address potential reconstruction error accumulation. | This is a borderline paper with mixed reviews. While reviewers agreed that VEGA effectively addresses a critical challenge in ECG analysis—poor cross-subject generalization—by creatively adapting 2D generative models to enrich the training manifold and align distributions, they also raised serious concerns about the paper’s soundness and significance: first, the empirical validation lacks comprehensive baselines, particularly comparisons with existing time-series augmentation techniques and alternative generative approaches, making it difficult to isolate VEGA’s unique contribution versus generic data expansion benefits; second, the assumption of label preservation during masked reconstruction is insufficiently validated, raising the risk of introducing noisy labels when critical pathological features are obscured; third, the evidence for generated sample diversity is purely qualitative and unsubstantiated, while the experimental design omits key comparisons, such as 1D generative baselines and alternative lead configurations. The rebuttal clarified certain procedural details but did not fully resolve concerns regarding novelty, baseline comparisons, diversity quantification, or label preservation validation. After careful deliberation, I lean a bit towards rejecting this manuscript. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal clarifies several key aspects of the method, particularly the sampling procedure, the role of the Frequency Adapter, and the rationale behind the cross-modal design. However, some limitations remain only partially resolved. In particular, the lack of direct comparisons with standard time-series augmentation techniques and 1D generative baselines in downstream tasks is still an important gap, and the evidence supporting generation diversity and label preservation remains somewhat indirect. Given the novelty of the cross-modal augmentation strategy and the consistent empirical improvements across tasks, the rebuttal sufficiently strengthens the paper. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal clarifies several methodological details and partially addresses concerns regarding model design, label preservation, and baseline comparisons. I appreciate the interesting idea of leveraging visual generative priors for ECG augmentation, and the reported empirical improvements suggest potential value. However, I still have some reservations about the core motivation: ECG is inherently a 1D periodic physiological signal with strong cycle- and morphology-specific constraints, and it remains insufficiently justified why a vision generative model should be more suitable than signal-specific generative models for this task. Overall, while this concern remains, I am willing to support acceptance given the novelty of the cross-modal formulation and the promising experimental results.
